sens: The first letter of the Greek alphabet
The number 1 in Greek numbering
The beginning, the origin of all things
The entirety, from beginning to end
G0001G.detail:
1. Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, just as it is the first letter of our alphabet. It is a simple letter, a written sign, but it opens the series of all other signs.

2. In ancient Greece, letters were also used to write numbers: alpha designated the number 1 (or 1000 if marked differently). It is the number of the beginning, the one that precedes all others.

3. In Revelation, Jesus says: "I am the alpha and the omega" (Revelation 1:8). Alpha symbolizes here the beginning, the starting point of creation, history, and everything that exists — the image of the Creator who initiates all things.

4. Together, "alpha and omega" (the first and the last letter) signify entirety, completeness. Christ encompasses everything: from the first moment to the last, nothing escapes him. That is why Revelation 21:6 also says: "the beginning and the end" — one and the same idea, expressed differently.
G0001G.origine: Alpha comes from ancient Greek and is related to the Hebrew aleph, which meant "head" or "chief." The very name of the letter evokes its role: it is the head of the alphabet, the one that comes first, the one that leads all others. This is why this word has naturally taken on spiritual meanings: the first, the original, the one who begins and governs.
G0001G.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, only in Revelation. Jesus uses it to describe himself in chapters 1, 21, and 22. Each time, he asserts that he is "the alpha and the omega" — a formula that emphasizes both his eternity (he was before all, he will be after all) and his absolute lordship (he masters all that exists). It is a very powerful affirmation of his divinity and supremacy over creation.
G0001G.portee: For the Christian reading Revelation, this symbol is a word of comfort and assurance. In the midst of tribulations and uncertainty, knowing that Christ is the alpha and the omega means that no event escapes his knowledge, no story surprises him, and everything converges toward his plan. It is a call to trust in his eternal sovereignty.

sens: Brother of Moses and first high priest of Israel
Ancestor of the Levitical priestly lineage
G0002.detail:
1. Aaron is the older brother of Moses, called by God to be the first high priest of Israel and intermediary between God and the people. It was to him that God commanded to offer sacrifices in the Tabernacle. His descendants formed the priestly class that served throughout the history of Israel, as indicated by the mention of the class of Abijah to which Zechariah belonged (Luke 1:5).
2. The priesthood of Aaron established a particular order of worship that the Epistle to the Hebrews contrasts with the superior order of Melchizedek fulfilled in Jesus Christ. Aaron's rod, which had miraculously budded, was kept in the ark of the covenant as a testimony of his divine calling (Hebrews 9:4), while the people questioned the authority he received from God (Acts 7:40).
G0002.origine: The name Aaron comes from the Hebrew אַהֲרוֹן (Aharon), whose original etymology is debated but could mean "the one who ascends" or "mountaineer." Aaron historically represents the founding figure of the Levitical priesthood in Israelite tradition. His name has remained emblematic of divine service organized according to the Mosaic Law.
G0002.emploi: Aaron is mentioned 5 times in the New Testament, always in reference to his role as the first high priest and founder of the priestly line. In the Gospel of Luke, Elizabeth is presented as belonging to the "daughters of Aaron," meaning she is a descendant of the priestly lineage (Luke 1:5). In Stephen's speech, Aaron represents the leader responsible for the idolatrous worship of the golden calf, revealing the people's unfaithfulness (Acts 7:40). The Epistle to the Hebrews uses him as a point of reference to show the superiority of Christ: while no one takes the honor of high priest for himself, but only when called by God, as Aaron was (Hebrews 5:4), Jesus surpasses this old order by being appointed according to the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 7:11). The objects of Aaronic worship, such as Aaron's budding rod, kept in the ark, testify to the old order now fulfilled and transcended (Hebrews 9:4).
G0002.portee: Aaron embodies for the believer the reality of the priesthood instituted by the Law — a holy and necessary service, but limited and temporary. His story teaches that even the closest servants of God can falter (as in the case of the golden calf), and that their ministry, though authentic, prefigured a perfect and eternal priesthood in Jesus Christ. Recognizing Aaron means accepting that the Old Testament progressively reveals the divine intention, culminating in the person of Christ.

sens: The angel who rules over the abyss, chief of the creatures of destruction
The Hebrew name literally means "destruction"
G0003.detail:
1. Abaddon is a celestial being who governs the abyss (the place of chaos and perdition). In Revelation 9:11, John describes him as "the angel of the abyss," the one who commands the destructive creatures of that place. The text specifies that it is a Hebrew name, while its Greek equivalent is "Apollyon," which also means "destroyer."

2. The word comes from Hebrew and etymologically means "destruction." In the Old Testament, the term referred to the abode of the dead, the place of ruin; here, in Revelation, it takes the form of a personal being, an angel who bears this significant name of his destructive role.
G0003.origine: The word comes directly from the Hebrew אֲבַדּוֹן (Abaddōn), derived from the root meaning "to perish," "to be destroyed." In the Greek Old Testament, this word was translated as ἀπώλεια (loss, destruction), particularly in the wisdom books like Job and Proverbs, where it referred to the abode of the dead or nothingness. John adopts it as a proper name to personify the angel who rules over this abyss of destruction.
G0003.emploi: Abaddon appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 9:11. John, in his vision of the eschatological plagues (the calamities of the end times), presents him as a specific celestial being: the angel of the abyss who commands the creatures of destruction that rise from that place. The text emphasizes that John gives the name in both languages — Hebrew and Greek — showing that this character was known under these two linguistic traditions of his time.
G0003.portee: This name reminds the reader that destruction and chaos are not disorder without a master: behind the forces of ruin acts a personal will. For the Christian, this illustrates the spiritual reality of the powers of evil and their limits: they strike only according to God's permission and for a determined time. It is a call to vigilance and trust in divine sovereignty over all events of the last days.

sens: that does not weigh down, that does not burden
that costs nothing, that does not require resources
that does not constitute a burden for someone
G0004.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the word refers to something light, which has no material weight. But Paul uses it figuratively to speak of a person who does not create difficulty or problems: in 2 Corinthians 11:9, he states that he has "kept himself from being a burden to you," meaning he did not want to become a financial weight or burden for the church in Corinth.
2. The word expresses the absence of burden or constraint: Paul wants his presence and ministry not to weigh on those who support him. This shows his concern not to exploit the generosity of the Corinthians, even though he had the right, as an apostle, to receive their support.
3. It is an attitude of delicacy and respect towards those who welcome him: not being a burden means not imposing his upkeep, but rather being a blessing and not a burden.
G0004.origine: The word comes from the Greek "baros" which means "weight" or "burden." The prefix "a" at the beginning (called the alpha privative) negates the word that follows: "abarès" thus literally means "without weight." This is a common Greek construction to form opposites: adding an "a" to say "not" or "without."
G0004.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:9. Paul uses it to express his pastoral principle: although he has the right to receive material support from the churches he founds (as he explains elsewhere), he often chooses to provide for his needs in other ways, so as not to be a burden. This term emphasizes his independence and love for the Corinthians: he prefers to be without burden rather than weigh on their finances. It is a concrete illustration of his apostolic humility.
G0004.portee: This word invites Christians to reflect on the balance between receiving what is due to us and showing delicacy towards those who support us. Paul models an attitude of responsibility and respect: accepting help when necessary, but also seeking to lighten the burden of others. For a leader or minister, this reminds us of the importance of not abusing the trust and generosity of those we accompany.

sens: Aramaic term of endearment and affection for father
G0005.detail: 1. "Abba" is the word an Aramaic child would use to call his father, just as a small French child says "papa." It is an intimate, personal term, filled with tenderness and trust. Jesus uses it in his prayer in the Garden of Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), showing how he addresses God his Father with absolute simplicity and familiarity. 2. Paul takes up this same word to describe the relationship of Christians to God: when the Holy Spirit dwells in us, we can cry out "Abba, Father!" (Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6), which means we have received the Spirit of adoption and can address God with the same trusting intimacy as a child speaking to his father.
G0005.origine: This word comes from Aramaic (the language spoken by the Jews at the time of Jesus), borrowed from a Semitic root that simply designates the father. In Hebrew, one says "av," but in Aramaic, "abba" is the emphatic or affectionate form. The apostles retained this Aramaic word even while writing in Greek, so significant was it for the disciples: it reminded them how Jesus himself spoke to God.
G0005.emploi: This word appears only three times in the New Testament, always accompanied by the Greek word "pater" (father), forming the expression "Abba, pater" — Abba being the cry of the heart, and pater the Greek word that explains to Greek readers what this Aramaic term means. In Mark 14:36, Jesus in Gethsemane prays Abba, demonstrating his filial intimacy even in the face of his impending passion. In Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6, Paul uses this cry to describe the privilege of believers: the Spirit allows them to cry out "Abba, Father!", a cry that expresses the assurance of their divine sonship and their inheritance in Christ.
G0005.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals the intimate nature of the relationship with God: it is not a cold distance or a servile obedience, but a filial trust, like that of a child who throws himself into his father's arms. Jesus invites us to this same familiarity with God. It is a promise of spiritual freedom and security in faith.

sens: the second son of Adam and Eve, a shepherd
the one whose sacrifice was accepted by God through faith
the innocent blood unjustly shed
the silent witness whose death cries out for justice
G0006.detail:
1. Abel is the younger son of Adam and Eve, presented in Genesis 4:2 as a keeper of sheep. His Hebrew name means "breath" or "vanity," evoking the brevity of life; he himself will die young, killed by his brother Cain.

2. What makes Abel great is his faith: Hebrews 11:4 emphasizes that "by faith Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice" than that of his brother. God approved his offerings, recognizing his righteous heart.

3. His blood, shed by Cain, becomes a symbol of the innocent blood unjustly spilled. Jesus cites him in Matthew 23:35 as the first righteous one murdered in sacred history, placed at the beginning of the long chain of martyrs.

4. In Hebrews 12:24, Abel's blood "still speaks" even though he is dead: it is an image of justice that cries out for vengeance and testimony in heaven. But the blood of Jesus "speaks better," bringing not condemnation but salvation and grace.
G0006.origine: The name Abel comes from the Hebrew hebel, which literally means "breath" or "vanity," expressing the ephemeral and fragile nature of human life. It is a deeply symbolic name: the boy carries within him, from birth, the destiny of mortality. His story establishes the biblical notion of a pleasing sacrifice to God and injustice towards the righteous.
G0006.emploi: Abel appears four times in the New Testament, always in a perspective of faith and justice. In Hebrews 11:4, he represents the model of the believer who offers his heart to God: his faith makes him righteous even before the Law is given. In Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51, Jesus cites him as the first unjustly killed martyr, whose blood cries out for justice. In Hebrews 12:24, his blood becomes a contrast: while Abel's blood demands vengeance, that of Jesus appeases divine wrath and brings us into the new covenant. Abel embodies the narrow and often persecuted path of true faith.
G0006.portee: Abel teaches us that true worship arises from faith, not zeal or appearance. His story poses an eternal question: why does God accept one brother's sacrifice and reject the other's? Because God looks at the heart. For the believer, Abel also reminds us that faith can be costly: it exposes one to jealousy and persecution. But his "word" that "still speaks" shows that God never forgets the cry of the righteous, and that Christ has transformed this cry for vengeance into a hymn of mercy.

sens: Son of Rehoboam, king of Judah
G0007G.detail: Abijah is the son of King Rehoboam and the grandson of King Solomon. He appears in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew, where he is named in the succession of kings: "Rehoboam begot Abijah; Abijah begot Asa" (Matthew 1:7). This Hebrew name means "the Lord is my father" and marks an important link in the royal line leading to the birth of the Messiah.
G0007G.origine: The name Abijah comes from the Hebrew אֲבִיָּה (Abiyyah), composed of two elements: "abi" (my father) and "Yah" (the Lord). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the divine name within it, expressing a personal relationship of the father with God. This type of name was common among the kings and priests of Israel.
G0007G.emploi: Abijah designates two important figures in biblical history. The first is the son of Rehoboam and king of Judah, mentioned here in the royal genealogy of Matthew 1:7. The second is a priest from the line of Eleazar, chief of a priestly division of the temple (mentioned in 1 Chronicles 24). The provided usage concerns only King Abijah, inserted in the genealogical chain that establishes the continuity between Solomon and Jesus Christ.
G0007G.portee: The mention of Abijah in the genealogy of Jesus reminds us that Christ comes from a true royal lineage. It shows how God has guided the history of Israel through the generations, despite the unfaithfulness of some kings. For the Christian reader, this affirms that Jesus comes from the house of David, fulfilling the messianic promises of the Old Testament.

sens: Son of King Rehoboam, ancestor of Jesus
G0007H.detail: Abia is the name of a king of Judah, son of Rehoboam. He appears in the genealogy of Jesus given in Matthew 1:7, where he holds a place among the ancestors of the Messiah. This name reminds us of how God has guided the history of Israel up to the coming of Christ.
G0007H.origine: The Hebrew name אֲבִיָּה (Abiyya) or אֲבִיָּהוּ (Abiyyahu) literally means "My Father is Yahweh": it is composed of the word for "father" and the divine name. It is a theophoric name, common in Israel, that expresses the relationship of the bearer with God. Several important figures in the Old Testament bore this name, including the king and the priest mentioned here.
G0007H.emploi: Abia refers to two different biblical personalities. First, a son of King Rehoboam who ruled over Judah, mentioned in 1 Kings 14:1 and who appears in the genealogy of Christ in Matthew 1:7, thus including the people of Judah in God's plan. Second, a priest of the lineage of Eleazar, whose priestly class bore his name; the Bible mentions that Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, belonged to this class of Abia (Luke 1:5), placing him among the Temple servants responsible for worship according to a rotation.
G0007H.portee: These two Abias remind us that God works through the ordinary history of kings and priests, guiding His people according to His plan. For the Christian reader, the genealogical Abia testifies that Jesus is part of a royal lineage established by God, while Abia the priest reminds us that Zechariah, though of modest rank, played a decisive role in welcoming the announcement of the birth of John the Baptist.

sens: High priest of Israel during the time of King David
G0008.detail: Abiathar is the high priest (chief priest) mentioned by Mark in Mark 2:26, when Jesus justifies His disciples for eating the showbread. Scripture shows him intervening at a key moment in the royal history of Israel.
G0008.origine: The Hebrew name אֶבְיָתָר (Ebiathar) probably means "my father excels" or "excellent genealogy." He is a historical figure from the Old Testament, documented in the historical books of Israel.
G0008.emploi: Mark mentions him only once, in Mark 2:26. Jesus invokes him as a biblical example: at the time of Abiathar, high priest under King David, David himself entered the sanctuary and ate the bread reserved for the priests, an act ordinarily forbidden. Jesus uses this to show that God's mercy surpasses ritual rules: if hungry David could eat this bread without sinning, because the need was urgent, then Jesus' disciples can also transcend the Sabbath when it is right.
G0008.portee: This passage teaches us that biblical rules are never absolute to the detriment of mercy and need. Jesus calls us to discern when the letter of the Law must yield to love and compassion.

sens: region of ancient Syria, at the foot of the Anti-Lebanon
G0009.detail: 1. Abilene is a mountainous region of ancient Near East, located in the foothills of the Anti-Lebanon (the range facing Lebanon), northeast of the Promised Land. It was governed as a tetrarchy, that is, a small principality ruled by a tetrarch. Luke mentions Lysanias as tetrarch of Abilene in the fifteenth year of the reign of the Roman emperor Tiberius (Luke 3:1).
G0009.origine: The Greek name "Abilene" comes from the Semitic and refers to a region of Syria. In antiquity, this region held a strategic position in the territories between the Mediterranean and the desert, governed by local princes under Roman control.
G0009.emploi: Abilene appears only once in the New Testament, in the chronological and geographical context that Luke provides at the beginning of his account of John the Baptist's ministry (Luke 3:1). By naming the different tetrarchs (Herod for Galilee, Philip for Iturea and Trachonitis, Lysanias for Abilene) and the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, Luke precisely situates the time and political context of his account, establishing the historical authority of his Gospel.
G0009.portee: This mention reminds the reader that Jesus came in a complex political context, where multiple powers coexisted: local princes and the Roman Empire. It also highlights Luke's historical rigor and the importance of placing the Gospel in reality, within a verifiable geography and chronology.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Matthew
G0010.detail: Abiud is a man mentioned only in the genealogy of Jesus according to the Gospel of Matthew. He is the son of Zerubbabel and the father of Eliakim, appearing in the chain of descendants from David to Jesus. His name appears only once, in Matthew 1:13, in this succession of generations that establishes the royal and Davidic lineage of Jesus.
G0010.origine: The Hebrew name אֲבִיָּהוּד (Abiyahou) literally means "My father is majesty" or "Father of majesty," composed of abi (father) and houdi or yahud (majesty, glory). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains a reference to God, like many Hebrew names in the Old Testament. The name was transmitted in Greek in the form Ἀβιούδ (Abioud).
G0010.emploi: Abiud is cited only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:13, in the genealogy of Jesus. He represents one of the generations of the return from exile (his father Zerubbabel was the leader of the return of the Hebrews from Babylon), and his inclusion in this lineage reminds us how God preserved the descendants of David through the darkest periods of Israel's history, up to the coming of the promised Messiah.

sens: Founding patriarch of the people of Israel, father of Isaac and Ishmael
Ancestor of all believers, symbol of faith in God
Central figure of the divine covenant with the Jewish people
G0011.detail: 1. Abraham is the quintessential patriarch in the Hebrew Bible. He is the man whom God called to leave his country to go to a promised land, and to whom He granted an innumerable descendants. Matthew 1:1 announces him at the beginning of the Gospel as the ancestor of Jesus Christ. 2. Beyond his simple biological lineage, Abraham embodies faith: he believed in God's promise even when everything seemed impossible. Romans 4:1-3 and Galatians 3:6-9 repeatedly refer to his act of believing, which made him righteous before God. 3. In the New Testament, being a "son of Abraham" or "of Abraham's offspring" does not primarily refer to a physical genealogy, but to a spiritual lineage — whoever believes as Abraham believed. Luke 13:16 refers to a woman with a disability as a "daughter of Abraham" not by blood, but because she belongs to this covenant people. John 8:37-39 clarifies that true offspring is not of blood: Jesus tells the Pharisees that having Abraham as an ancestor is not enough if they do not do the works of Abraham, which means faith.
G0011.origine: The Hebrew name אַבְרָהָם (Abraham) literally means "father of a multitude": "ab" = father, "hamon" = multitude. This name was given to him by God Himself when the covenant was established (Genesis 17:5). It is a name that summarizes the entire divine promise: despite his old age and his wife's barrenness, Abraham would become the father of a lineage that would cover the earth. The Greek word Ἀβραάμ (Abraam) simply transcribes this Hebrew name into the language of the New Testament.
G0011.emploi: Abraham appears 69 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Luke, John), in the letter to the Romans, and in Galatians. Matthew introduces him in verse 1:1 to establish the genealogy of Jesus. The Gospels of Luke and John frequently return to this name, particularly in debates: the Pharisees claim to descend from Abraham (John 8:33), but Jesus confronts them by showing that true offspring is that of faith, not of blood. The letter to the Romans uses Abraham as a model of justification by faith (Romans 4 in its entirety). Galatians 3 and 4 invoke him to show that the covenant with Abraham is fulfilled in Jesus Christ and extends to all believers, including Gentiles. Hebrews 11 presents him among the great men of faith in the Old Testament. Each usage reinforces the idea that the New Testament reinterprets Abraham not as a carnal glory or genealogical pride, but as the prototype of the believer.
G0011.portee: Knowing Abraham means understanding what it truly means to believe in God and to be saved. His life shows that one becomes a child of God neither by blood nor by the law, but by faith. This is the very teaching that Paul explicitly draws from Abraham in Romans 4: justification comes from trusting in God's word, not from works of the flesh. For every Christian, Abraham is the spiritual father from whom we inherit the blessing not by genealogy, but by imitating his faith in Jesus Christ.

sens: Bottomless depth, unfathomable abyss
The deep waters of the sea at the creation of the world
The abode of the dead, underground region
The dwelling place of demons and evil spirits
That which is distant, inaccessible to man
G0012.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a depth that is impossible to measure, an unfathomable abyss. It is the image of a terrifying and empty immensity: one thinks of an open well without a bottom where looking down induces vertigo. In Revelation 9:2, John sees smoke rising "from the pit of the abyss": this is that infinite chasm.

2. In the creation narrative, the abyss is the chaos of primordial waters that covers the earth before God creates order. It is the oceanic depth, vast and untamed, before the appearance of life.

3. The abyss also becomes the underground world of the dead, the hidden place beneath our feet where the deceased rest, far from the living world. In Romans 10:7, Paul refers to descending into the abyss to bring Christ up from the dead: it is the realm of death, invisible and distant.

4. For biblical writers, the abyss is especially the prison of demons and evil creatures. In Luke 8:31, the demons beg Jesus not to send them into the abyss: they fear being confined and tormented there. In Revelation 9:11, a wicked angel reigns over the abyss like a king over his underground domain. It is a place of punishment and confinement for evil.

5. Figuratively, it refers to what is beyond human reach, what cannot be explored or mastered.
G0012.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "bottomless" (composed of the prefix "a-" = without, and "bussos" = depth). In Hebrew, the abyss is called "tehom", a word that designates the primordial waters of chaos. The Greek translators of the Old Testament chose the word "abussos" to convey this idea of limitless depth. It is an evocative word: it paints the image of a vast and terrifying void.
G0012.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mainly in Revelation and in Paul. Luke (8:31) shows the demons terrified at the thought of being thrown into the abyss, which reveals that it is for them a form of punishment or imprisonment. Paul (Romans 10:7) uses the abyss as an image of the abode of the dead to speak of the resurrection of Christ. But it is Revelation that enriches the meaning the most: the abyss appears there as the pit from which evil spirits escape (9:1-2), ruled by the angel Abaddon (9:11), and from which the beast emerges to make war against the saints (11:7, 17:8). Towards the end, the abyss is sealed (20:1, 20:3) to prevent Satan from misleading the nations. It is always a fearsome and closed place, associated with evil and the underground mystery.
G0012.portee: Understanding the abyss helps the reader grasp how the Bible views the invisible world: a hidden domain, governed by spiritual forces hostile to God, but under His absolute control. For the believer, the abyss serves as a reminder that evil has a limit and a judgment; it is never beyond God's reach. The resurrection of Christ, mentioned in Romans 10:7, shows that Christ has conquered death and the abyss: there is nothing that the believer needs to fear.

sens: Prophet of the first Christian century who foretold the future by the Holy Spirit
G0013.detail: 1. Agabus is a Jewish prophet from the time of the apostles. He appears twice in the Acts: first in Antioch, where he predicts a great famine that will occur under Emperor Claudius (Acts 11:28), and then in Caesarea, where he symbolically announces the sufferings that Paul would endure in Jerusalem (Acts 21:10). His prophecies are not his own thoughts, but words inspired by the Holy Spirit that he communicates to the church.
G0013.origine: The name Agabus does not have a clear established Hebrew or Greek etymology. It is a name borne by this particular man, known only through these two mentions in the Acts of the Apostles.
G0013.emploi: Agabus appears only twice in the New Testament, always in Acts. In Acts 11:28, he is presented as one of the prophets who came from Antioch to Jerusalem, who rises to announce by the Spirit a future famine. This prophecy is historically verified during the reign of Claudius. In Acts 21:10, he intervenes again, this time in Caesarea, to prophetically warn Paul of the chains and sufferings that await him. In both cases, Agabus exercises the gift of prophecy, speaking in the name of the Holy Spirit and not of himself.
G0013.portee: Agabus reminds us that in the early church, the Holy Spirit spoke through prophets to guide, warn, and confirm the faith of God's people. His existence shows that the prophetic charism was alive and active, and that God was preparing His servants for the trials to come. For the reader, it is a lesson on the importance of believing in the warnings that God gives through His servants.

sens: to perform benevolent and generous actions
to show kindness through concrete gestures
to provide for the needs of others with liberality
G0014.detail:
1. To do good means to perform actions that manifest kindness: generous and benevolent gestures towards others. In Acts 14:17, Paul describes God Himself as one who "continues to bear witness to what He is by doing good," through rains, fruitful seasons, and abundant food — God generously provides for everyone's needs.
2. The verb also refers to the action of actively and visibly showing kindness. In 1 Timothy 6:18, Paul urges the rich to "do good," which is accompanied by being "rich in good works," having "liberality, generosity" — it is a generosity that translates into concrete acts towards others.
G0014.origine: The word comes from the combination of two Greek roots: "agathos" (good) and "ergon" (work, action). Thus, "to do good" literally means "to produce a good work." This composition expresses the idea that goodness is not just a feeling, but a visible and effective action. The word is rare in the New Testament and belongs to the vocabulary of moral exhortation.
G0014.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament, always to describe a generous and benevolent action. In Acts 14:17, it is God who "does good" by providing for human needs — rains, food, joy. In 1 Timothy 6:18, it is the exhortation addressed to wealthy Christians to "do good," practice good works and generosity. In both cases, the verb emphasizes the concrete and observable nature of goodness: it must manifest through acts.
G0014.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that goodness is not a vague good intention, but an active commitment. Seeing God Himself described as one who "does good" (in Acts) shows that generosity is a reflection of the divine nature. For the Christian, especially one who has resources, the exhortation to "do good" invites transforming faith into concrete gestures of liberality and help towards others.

sens: To perform a good, just, and useful action
To act for the benefit of another person
To do good even to those who do us harm
To practice good as an expression of God's will
G0015.detail:
1. The verb refers to the concrete action of doing something good: not just having good intentions, but acting. In Luke 6:9, Jesus asks if it is lawful to "do good" on the Sabbath, meaning to heal, to save a life — a beneficial and just action.
2. Good can be done for the benefit of another person: in Luke 6:33, Jesus asks His disciples to do good even to those who do good to them, to move beyond simple reciprocity.
3. The radical extension of the command appears in Luke 6:35: to love one's enemies, to do good, to lend without expecting anything in return — this is the sign that one resembles the Most High, who is good to the ungrateful and the wicked.
4. In 1 Peter, doing good is presented as God's will (2:15) and a virtue even under persecution: enduring mistreatment while doing what is right is a "grace before God" (2:20). It is a faithful practice that transforms the Christian testimony.
G0015.origine: The word comes from the combination of "agathos" (good) and "poieō" (to do). It literally means "to do-good." In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), this verb translates the Hebrew "yatab" in the intensive form, which expresses the idea of treating someone well, of doing good to them. It is a compound verb that emphasizes the concrete action of good, not the state or abstract quality.
G0015.emploi: This verb appears eight times in the New Testament, mainly in Luke and Peter. In Luke, particularly in the Sermon on the Plain (6:9, 33, 35), Jesus teaches a radical ethic: doing good goes beyond simple legal justice (healing on the Sabbath is permitted) and ordinary reciprocity (doing good to those who return it). In Peter, the verb fits into the exhortation to the persecuted: doing good silences the ignorant (2:15), it is a grace to endure for this (2:20), and it characterizes obedient children of God (3:6). The context of early Christianity is that of a minority living its ethics under tension and opposition.
G0015.portee: This word calls the Christian to move from good intention to concrete beneficial action. It broadens the perspective: doing good is not limited to friends or allies, but radically extends to enemies and the ungrateful, reflecting the goodness of the Father. Under suffering and injustice, persevering in good is recognized as grace and a powerful testimony. It is a call to a coherent and generous ethical life, rooted in the nature of God Himself.

sens: The action of doing good, practicing kindness
The moral virtue of acting correctly and justly
G0016.detail:
1. The action of doing good, practicing kindness: it is to accomplish what is right and good, especially in difficult circumstances. In 1 Peter 4:19, Christians who suffer are encouraged to "do what is good" by entrusting their souls to the faithful Creator — even in the face of persecution, they continue to act with righteousness.
2. The moral virtue of acting correctly and justly: it is a disposition of the heart to do good, which goes beyond simple isolated acts and becomes a habitual way of living.
G0016.origine: The word comes from the Greek "agathos" (good) and "poiéô" (to do, to accomplish): it literally means "to do-good," or "to do the good." It belongs to the family of "agathon" (the good) and "agathos" (good). This simple composition reflects the idea that good is not an abstract quality, but a concrete action, a daily practice.
G0016.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 4:19. In this context, the apostle Peter exhorts persecuted Christians to persevere in doing good, entrusting their fate to God. The word emphasizes that Christian virtue is not passive: it consists of continuing to act with righteousness and kindness, even when suffering makes it less appealing.
G0016.portee: This notion reminds Christians that doing good is not optional or conditional — it is a duty that persists even amid trials. It encourages seeing doing good not as a series of isolated good works, but as a constant commitment to God and neighbor, rooted in trust in His love.

sens: one who acts with kindness and righteousness
one who performs good deeds
one who practices good
G0017.detail: 1. The word literally designates one who "does good" — it refers to a person whose actions are marked by kindness and moral uprightness. In 1 Peter 2:14, the apostle Peter speaks of "good people," those whom civil authorities are called to approve; these are those whose conduct is righteous and benevolent. 2. It is one who concretely accomplishes good deeds, not just in intention but in action. Such a person manifests through their gestures and behavior that they seek the good of others and the honor of God. 3. The word emphasizes one who habitually practices good — it is a character trait, a lasting orientation of life, not an isolated act.
G0017.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "agathos" (good) and "poieo" (to do, to make). It literally means "one who does good." It is the opposite of the term "kakopoios" (one who does evil). The notion of "good" here is not abstract: it refers to what is right, useful, in accordance with the order established by God.
G0017.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 2:14. Peter uses it to refer to citizens who conduct themselves well and whose righteousness deserves recognition by those in authority. The context shows that Peter exhorts Christians to submit to human authorities, and he asserts that these authorities are established to punish wrongdoers and approve good people — that is, those who do good.
G0017.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the Christian life is not self-contained: it must be manifested through visible and recognizable acts of good. It is a call to practical righteousness, to conduct such that even those who do not share the faith recognize the moral quality of the Christian. This encourages seeking approval, not out of weakness, but out of integrity.

sens: That which possesses excellent quality, complete in itself
That which produces satisfaction, benefit, or pleasure
That which is morally right, in accordance with the will of God
That which is benevolent, full of kindness towards others
That which is useful, beneficial, or advantageous
Goods, material possessions or spiritual blessings
G0018.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what is excellent in its nature or function — a good tree bears good fruit (Matthew 7:18), good soil produces a beautiful harvest (Luke 8:8). It is the complete, finished quality that satisfies.
2. It qualifies what brings good, advantage to the one who receives it: the gifts of the heavenly Father are good because they fulfill us (Matthew 7:11), the good portion that Mary chose at Jesus' feet is truly beneficial to her (Luke 10:42).
3. The moral sense appears strongly: the good is what pleases God, what is in accordance with His will. This is why we discern the will of God as "what is good, acceptable, and perfect" (Romans 12:2), and why doing good is fulfilling what God approves (Romans 12:21).
4. The word also expresses an affective quality, a kindness, a natural benevolence. A good friend, a good heart: it is a sweetness of character, an inclination to do good.
5. It applies to everything that is truly beneficial and desirable — a good reputation (1 Thessalonians 3:6), a good news that saves.
6. In the plural, goods refer to material possessions (Luke 12:18) or the spiritual advantages that God grants us (Hebrews 9:11).
G0018.origine: The Greek word agathos comes from a very ancient root that evokes the idea of perfect adaptation, of what fits and fulfills its function well. In Hebrew, the Old Testament Greek translates it mainly as tôb, which also means "good" in the sense of "beautiful," "pleasant," "useful." The word belongs to a fundamental moral family of the New Testament, alongside "kindness" (agathôsunê) and "to do good" (agathourgéô).
G0018.emploi: The word appears 91 times in the New Testament, mainly in the writings of Luke and Paul. It qualifies very diverse realities: God Himself is good (Mark 10:18), His actions are good, His will is good (Romans 12:2). Faithful servants perform good works (Ephesians 2:10, 2 Timothy 2:21). A good conscience, a good reputation, a good portion — everything that is in accordance with the good of God. The word clearly opposes evil, sin, and what is bad (ponèros, kakos). Paul often uses it to exhort Christians to "seek good" (Galatians 6:10) and to "do good" (Romans 2:10, Ephesians 4:28). In Luke, it characterizes the visible fruits of faith: good soil receives the seed, a good heart keeps it.
G0018.portee: For the Christian, this word invites us to distinguish true good — what pleases God and truly builds up — from evil or attractive falsehood. It reminds us that God Himself is the absolute good, the source of all that is good. Finally, it urges the believer to cultivate good works, not out of legal obligation, but from a transformed heart that naturally seeks the good of God and of others.

sens: Disposition of the heart that drives one to do good
Quality of one who desires the good of others with gentleness and generosity
Concrete manifestation of this benevolence in words and actions
G0019.detail:
1. Kindness is primarily an inner disposition, an orientation of the heart towards good. When Paul says that the Romans are "full of goodness" (Romans 15:14), he speaks of this capacity to wish well to others, naturally inclined towards encouragement and help.
2. It also manifests as a stable personal quality, distinguished from justice which is firmer: where justice demands what is due, kindness adds softness, generosity, almost tenderness. It is the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22, alongside love and joy.
3. Concretely, kindness produces acts: "good intentions" (2 Thessalonians 1:11), words that comfort and build up. It does not stop at good intention; it acts, it gives, it accompanies.
G0019.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἀγαθός (agathós), which means "good." The suffix -σύνη (-sunē) creates an abstract noun, as one would make "justice" from "just." In Hebrew from the Old Testament, this word mainly translates טוֹבָה (touvah) and its forms, which express the goodness, benevolence, and the good that a king or God grants to His people. It is a divine quality transferred to the heart of one who walks with God.
G0019.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, always in the writings of Paul. In Romans 15:14, it designates the state of the Christian filled with kindness. In Galatians 5:22, it is listed among the fruits of the Spirit, as a virtue that the Holy Spirit develops in us. In Ephesians 5:9, it characterizes the fruit of light, what the new life in Christ produces. Finally, in 2 Thessalonians 1:11, Paul prays that God will fulfill the "good intentions" of His kindness: this refers to God's generous and merciful intentions towards His children. Each time, kindness appears as a quality that unites firmness and softness, justice and mercy.
G0019.portee: Kindness invites the Christian to cultivate in themselves, through the Spirit, this generous and benevolent disposition towards others. It is not weakness; it is a strength that knows how to combine moral demand (justice) with tenderness towards the one who is weak. Meditating on God's kindness towards us, in His "good intentions," teaches us to become bearers of this same fruit in our relationships.

sens: lively and exuberant joy
leaping for joy
rejoicing in the face of a happy event
exultation of the heart
G0020.detail:
1. Joy is an intense and overflowing happiness, an exultation that seizes the whole being. It is not a calm and composed joy, but one that expresses itself with fervor and liveliness. Luke 1:44 gives a striking image: the child John the Baptist leaps for joy in Elizabeth's womb, as if joy shook him throughout his body at the approach of the Messiah.
2. It is also the joy that arises from good news or a favorable event. In Luke 1:14, the announcement of John the Baptist's birth will be a source of joy for Zechariah: the couple's barrenness will be overcome, a divine promise is fulfilled.
3. In moments of communion and celebration, joy characterizes the heart of the believer. Acts 2:46 shows the early Christians breaking bread with joy and gladness: it is a shared rejoicing, that of the people of God discovering themselves united in faith.
4. Joy can also refer to the divine anointing that fills the heart of the one chosen by God. In Hebrews 1:9, God anoints Christ with the oil of gladness, a figure of the Spirit that fills the one God establishes.
G0020.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb ἀγαλλιάω (agalliaô), which literally means "to rejoice with exuberance," "to exult." The root evokes a movement of the soul that bursts forth, a joy that overflows. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew גִּיל (gil), which expresses jubilation, the joy that makes the heart leap. It is a joy more intense and expressive than simple joy (χαρά, chara): it carries within it a movement, an outward manifestation.
G0020.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles. In Luke 1:14 and 1:44, it colors the events of the Annunciation: the birth of the Forerunner is associated with joyful joy. In Acts 2:46, it is the characteristic joy of the life of the early Church, that of brotherly communion and the breaking of bread. In Hebrews 1:9, it describes the divine joy that fills Christ. In Jude 1:24, joy is the final joy of the believer preserved and presented without blame before divine glory. Each context emphasizes that this joy springs from an encounter with God's action: promised birth, Holy Spirit, divine election, granted salvation.
G0020.portee: Joy reminds the Christian that faith is not austere, but alive and overflowing. It is a joy that arises from trust in God's work and manifests itself in daily life: in family (the joy of the fulfillment of His promises), in the Church (brotherly communion), before God Himself (the exultation of the heart seized by His grace). It invites the believer not to stifle their joy, but to let it express itself, both through gratitude and through celebration with others.

sens: To experience great joy, a deep gladness
To exult, to leap for joy at good news or a source of happiness
To find joy in someone or something
To glorify, to rejoice inwardly in an intense and manifest way
G0021.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to experience great joy, a gladness that overflows from the heart. It is a joy stronger than simple satisfaction: it is exultant, manifest. In Luke 10:21, Jesus "leaped for joy by the Holy Spirit" upon seeing the revelation of the Father to the children—His joy was so intense that it manifested physically.
2. The word particularly expresses the joy of one who rejoices IN something or IN someone, a joy that takes root in an object or person. Mary in Luke 1:47 declares: "my spirit rejoices in God, my Savior"—her joy springs from her relationship with God.
3. Rejoicing can even be expressed in the face of persecution, for it rests not on circumstances, but on what one believes. Matthew 5:12 calls to rejoice when suffering persecution, for the heavenly reward outweighs it.
4. Abraham "leaped for joy" (John 8:56) at seeing the day of Christ from afar—the word captures that soul's impulse that greets the fulfillment of the divine promise.
G0021.origine: The Greek word ἀγαλλιάω (agalliaō) comes from a root that expresses the idea of jumping, of impulse, of jubilation. Its older relative is ἀγάλλω (agallō), "to glorify." In Hebrew, it primarily translates גיל (gil), which means to rejoice, and רנן (rinnēn), which expresses a joy that manifests itself, a cry of joy. The basic image is that of a joy that makes the soul burst forth or leap.
G0021.emploi: The verb appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles of Peter. Matthew and Luke use it to describe joy in the face of salvation and divine blessings (Matthew 5:12, Luke 1:47, Luke 10:21). John connects it to hope and the promises of Christ (John 5:35, John 8:56). Acts uses it for the joy of the filled heart (Acts 2:26, Acts 16:34). Peter emphasizes that Christian joy persists even in trial (1 Peter 1:6, 1 Peter 1:8, 1 Peter 4:13). Revelation 19:7 announces eternal rejoicing at the marriage of the Lamb. The word always denotes a deep and vibrant joy, never a superficial joy.
G0021.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals that biblical joy is not a fragile emotion tied to circumstances, but an impulse of the soul based on God, His faithfulness, and His promises. Even in the face of suffering, the believer can "rejoice" because their trust rests on the Lord. This rejoicing also manifests intimacy with God: one only truly "rejoices" in the one they love and believe in. It is the expression of living faith.

sens: State of one who is not married
Freedom to devote oneself entirely to God without marital distraction
G0022.detail:
1. Unmarried describes the state of celibacy, the absence of marital ties: it is not having a husband or wife. In 1 Corinthians 7:8, Paul speaks to "those who are unmarried" and to widows, encouraging them to remain in this state like him. The word simply denotes the civil status of the person, man or woman.
2. Beyond simple celibacy, the word takes on a spiritual dimension in Paul: the unmarried can "care about the things of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:32), while one who has chosen marriage must also think about their spouse's needs. The absence of marriage offers a concentration of the soul towards God.
G0022.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: the prefix "a" (negation, "not") and "gamos" (marriage, union). It literally means "without marriage." The word belongs to a small family of Greek terms around marriage: we also find "endogamy" (marriage within a group) or derivatives like "monogamy." In the Greek Old Testament, this word is very rare; Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians to speak of those who have not entered into a marital union.
G0022.emploi: Paul uses this word only in 1 Corinthians 7, in his teaching on marriage and celibacy. The term appears four times (verses 8, 11, 32, 34) and concerns both men and women. Paul does not judge celibacy as superior to marriage, but recognizes that it offers a spiritual advantage: the unmarried have a freer spirit to serve the Lord. In 1 Corinthians 7:11, the word also describes the state of one who, separated from their spouse, should not remarry. The usage remains consistent: it always concerns the absence of current marital ties.
G0022.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that marriage and celibacy are both gifts from God, each with its responsibilities and graces. For the unmarried, it reminds that this state is not a curse, but an opportunity to give oneself entirely to God. Paul does not force anyone into celibacy: he simply affirms that if one can remain unmarried, they gain in freedom to serve the Lord. It is a call to serenity, not disenchantment.

sens: To feel a strong irritation, a anger mixed with disappointment in response to something that seems unjust, inappropriate, or outrageous
To express loudly one's dissatisfaction or emotional reaction
G0023.detail:
1. To be indignant means to feel a anger that springs from within when judging something unacceptable or offensive. It is a strong emotion, a feeling of injustice or disappointment: thus, the ten disciples "were indignant against the two brothers" (Matthew 20:24) because James and John seemed to them to be stealing places of honor. The chief priests also "were indignant" when they saw Jesus heal and the children praise Him (Matthew 21:15), because it clashed with their religious expectations.
2. To be indignant can also mean to actively express, manifest this dissatisfaction, to make it known loudly or in words: when we see "some expressing their indignation among themselves" about the perfume poured on Jesus (Mark 14:4), they are verbalizing their reaction, they are at least internally shouting it out.
G0023.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "much" (ἄγαν) and "to grieve, to be saddened." It thus evokes intense affliction, a sorrow that rises to indignation. It is an expressive word, making visible the turmoil of the heart. It appears especially in moments when biblical characters react strongly to acts or words.
G0023.emploi: This verb appears seven times in the New Testament, all occurrences in the Gospels. It describes emotional reactions to situations deemed unacceptable: the indignation of the ten apostles at the ambition of James and John (Matthew 20:24, Mark 10:41), that of the religious leaders at the miracles of Jesus (Matthew 21:15), that of the disciples at the waste of the perfume (Matthew 26:8, Mark 14:4). Remarkably, Jesus Himself "was indignant" when He saw His disciples rebuff the little children (Mark 10:14), showing that indignation is not always blameworthy — it can be just when it responds to an injustice. The context changes: sometimes it is a bad indignation (selfishness of the apostles), sometimes a good one (Jesus before the rejection of the children).
G0023.portee: This word shows us that emotion has its place in the life of the heart — even Jesus is indignant. But it also invites us to examine the source of our anger: to be indignant for pride or personal interest is blameworthy, while to be indignant in the face of injustice or what hinders the Kingdom reflects a rightful sensitivity. It is a call to have a right heart and pure motivations.

sens: A feeling of anger and disgust in response to something wrong or unjust
A strong reaction of rejection or condemnation
An outward manifestation of disapproval
G0024.detail:
1. Indignation is the deep feeling of anger and repugnance experienced in response to what is wrong, unjust, or offensive: it is the reaction of the heart that refuses to accept evil. In 2 Corinthians 7:11, Paul describes how godly sorrow produced indignation in the Corinthians: they rose up internally against the sin they had committed, rejecting it forcefully.
2. This word also describes how this inner anger manifests through actions: it becomes a power that drives one to act to correct what is wrong. Indignation drives one to punish evil, to restore justice, to stand firmly against sin.
G0024.origine: The word comes from the verb ἀγανακτέω (aganakteo), which literally means "to be very angry, to revolt." It is composed of an intensive prefix and a root that evokes rupture, diversion: the one who is indignant turns their heart away from the evil they see. It is a strong feeling that does not tolerate injustice.
G0024.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 7:11. Paul uses it to describe one of the positive fruits of "godly sorrow": when the Corinthians learned that they had committed a serious fault, this rightful awareness pushed them not only to be sad but to revolt against the sin itself, to reject it with indignation. It is a sign that their repentance was authentic and deep.
G0024.portee: The indignation that the Bible values here is not selfish anger or resentment, but the rightful reaction of the regenerated heart in the face of evil. It shows that true repentance transforms not only our thoughts but our emotions: we learn to hate what God hates. It is a lesson for every Christian: it is healthy to be indignant in the face of injustice and sin, provided that this indignation drives us towards correction and righteousness, and not towards vengeance or pride.

sens: to love with a giving love, to want the good of the other
to cherish, to have affection for
to attach one's heart to something (in a bad way: to love darkness, the world)
G0025.detail:
1. To love with a giving love. It is the love that chooses to want the good of the other, even when they do not deserve it: "For God so loved the world that He gave His only Son" (John 3:16). This love does not depend on what one feels; it is proven by actions.
2. To love God and one's neighbor. Jesus summarizes all the Law with this verb: to love God with all one's heart and one's neighbor as oneself (Matthew 22:37-39). He even asks to love one's enemies (Matthew 5:44).
3. To attach one's heart to something. The same verb can describe a bad attachment: men "preferred darkness to light" (John 3:19), or the Pharisees who "love the best seats" (Luke 11:43). What one loves reveals what governs the heart.
G0025.origine: Verb of the same family as ἀγάπη (love) and ἀγαπητός (beloved). Rare and rather dull in classical Greek, where it mainly means "to welcome with affection, to be content with," it becomes in the Septuagint the ordinary verb to translate the Hebrew אָהַב (to love). The New Testament fills it with a new meaning based on the love of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
G0025.emploi: With over a hundred occurrences, it is the great verb of love in the New Testament, especially in John (Gospel and epistles) and Paul. It expresses God's love for the world (John 3:16), the Father's love for the Son (John 3:35), and Christ's love for His own (John 13:1). It also carries the double commandment: to love God with all one's heart and one's neighbor as oneself (Matthew 22:37-39), extending even to loving one's enemies (Matthew 5:44). With a bad object, it designates the attachment of the heart: to love darkness (John 3:19) or the world (1 John 2:15).
G0025.portee: ἀγαπάω does not primarily describe a feeling, but a love that chooses to give for the good of the other. Its source is in God: "we love Him because He first loved us" (1 John 4:19). To love in this way becomes the mark of the disciple: "Love one another; as I have loved you" (John 13:34).

sens: Voluntary and benevolent love towards another person
Spiritual bond of love between God and humans, or among Christians
God's love for humanity and for Christ
Christ's love for humanity
Disposition of heart that drives one to serve and build up others
Shared meals among Christians, animated by this mutual love
G0026.detail: 1. Charity is primarily a sincere affection, a willful act that chooses to love another person without expecting a reward. It is a love that is benevolent and esteems its object (John 13:35: "By this all will know that you are My disciples, if you have love for one another"). 2. It denotes the unique spiritual bond of love that characterizes the relationships between God and His children, or among Christians themselves, in Christ (1 John 3:17: "But whoever has this world's goods, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart from him, how does the love of God abide in him?"). 3. Charity is also the love that God has for humanity and for Christ (Romans 5:8: "But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us"). 4. It is expressed in the love that Christ showed by giving Himself for His own (Romans 8:35: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?"). 5. Charity compels the believer to build up, comfort, and serve their brothers with a humble and patient attitude (1 Corinthians 8:1: "Knowledge puffs up, but charity edifies"). 6. In some passages, the word also refers to the festive meals shared by the early Christians, animated by this spirit of mutual love (Jude 1:12).
G0026.origine: The Greek word agapē comes from a root that expresses the idea of choosing, preferring. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (called the Septuagint), this word translates the Hebrew ahavah (אַהֲבָה), love in the broadest sense. The early Christians adopted this Greek term precisely because it emphasized a chosen, deliberate love, rather than a spontaneous feeling: it is the love that decides to love, even without a natural bond. It is distinctly different from the word philía (friendship), storgé (natural affection among close ones), and éros (carnal desire), which never appears in the New Testament.
G0026.emploi: The word charity appears 104 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Pauline and Johannine epistles. Paul uses it to describe the love that God has shown toward humanity (Romans 5:8), the love that Christians should have for one another (Romans 13:10), and this virtue as the foundation of all Christian life (1 Corinthians 13, which offers its incomparable portrait). John emphasizes charity as a sign of belonging to God and the presence of the Spirit (John 13:35; 1 John 3:17). The word can denote love as a feeling and bond (Romans 8:35), or as a concrete action, which drives one to care for a brother in need (1 Corinthians 8:1, where it "edifies"). In Jude 1:12, it also refers to a communion meal. Charity always appears in the Bible as the fruit of the Spirit, the mark of a disciple of Christ, and the glue of the Christian community.
G0026.portee: For the Christian, charity is much more than a feeling: it is a voluntary decision to love according to God, rooted in the very love that God has shown in Christ. It transforms the relationship with others (close or distant) into a true new life. Recognizing charity as the heart of faith helps the believer to go beyond rules and appearances to seek what truly builds others up and reflects the love of Christ.

sens: One who is loved, cherished
One who is loved by God
One who is loved by Christians, among brothers and sisters
Term of affection used to address someone one loves
That which is precious, dear to the heart
G0027.detail:
1. The word fundamentally designates a loved, cherished person. It is the state or quality of one who receives love. In Matthew 3:17, the Father calls Jesus "My beloved Son," expressing His absolute and eternal love for Him.

2. God loves believers with a special and free love. In Romans 1:7, Paul speaks of the Christians in Rome as "beloved of God." It is God's electing love that chooses and adopts them.

3. Christians love one another in the communion of the Church. In 1 Corinthians 4:14, Paul calls his disciples "beloved," showing that he truly cherishes them as a father. This affection is the fruit of shared love in the Body of Christ.

4. The word serves as a warm and respectful term of address. In 1 Peter 4:12, Peter addresses his readers: "Beloved, do not be surprised." It is a tender way of speaking to those one loves and wishes to protect.

5. Figuratively, that which is dear, precious. In Romans 11:28, the Jews are described as "beloved for the sake of their fathers": they remain infinitely precious to God despite their temporary rejection.
G0027.origine: The word comes from the verb ἀγαπάω (agapao), "to love," particularly the generous, free, unconditional love that characterizes divine love. The adjective beloved is therefore one who is the object of this special love. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew words יָדִיד (yedid) or יָתִיד (yatid), which denote one who is cherished, adored. It is a word full of affection and tenderness.
G0027.emploi: This word appears about 60 times in the New Testament, especially in the epistles. It is first encountered to describe the relationship of God with Jesus Christ (Matthew 3:17, Mark 1:11): Jesus is the beloved Son of the Father, which expresses His divine identity and the eternal love of the Father. Paul and the other apostles frequently use it to address Christians as a community beloved of God (Romans 1:7) and one another (1 Corinthians 4:14; 1 Peter 4:12). It is a term of affectionate greeting, especially at the beginning or during the epistles. The word also emphasizes election: those who are beloved of God are His chosen ones, set apart for Him. By contrast, in Romans 11:28, Paul notes that unbelieving Jews remain beloved despite their temporary rejection: this shows the perseverance of divine love beyond present rejection.
G0027.portee: This word reveals the heart of the Gospel: the selfless and eternal love of God. The believer who knows they are beloved of God is assured of their infinite worth, not by their merits but by grace. This certainty frees from doubt and guilt. Among Christians, the term reminds us that our mutual love reflects the love received from God; it creates a brotherhood aware of its divine foundation. Finally, the persistence of this term even towards those who reject God shows that God's love precedes and surpasses our responses.

sens: Egyptian servant of Abraham, mother of Ishmael
Allegorical figure of the Old Covenant and the bondage of the Law
G0028.detail:
1. Hagar is the Egyptian servant whom Abraham took as a wife according to the customs of his time (Genesis 16), and who bore Ishmael. She is a real woman from patriarchal history, mother of the Ishmaelite people.

2. The Apostle Paul uses Hagar as an allegorical figure in his letter to the Galatians (4:24-25): he sees in her and her son an image of the Old Covenant established at Mount Sinai, that of the Law which brings bondage. In contrast to Sarah (Abraham's free wife), Hagar represents spiritual bondage, while the children born of this covenant are "in bondage" to legal observances.
G0028.origine: The name Hagar comes from the Hebrew הָגָר (Hagar). The Septuagint (Greek version of the Old Testament) transcribes this name into Greek. Hagar means in Hebrew "flight" or "she who flees," which evokes her personal story: she flees from Egypt to the promised land. The name carries the drama of this excluded woman, but also the image of a deliverance in progress.
G0028.emploi: Hagar is mentioned twice in the New Testament, only by Paul in Galatians 4:24-25. Paul does not use this name to recount the story — his readers already know Genesis 16 — but to draw a spiritual meaning from it. He makes it an allegory of the two covenants: Hagar and Sinai on one side (the Law, bondage), Sarah and the heavenly Jerusalem on the other (the promise, freedom). This allegorical choice does not deny the historical reality of Hagar, but recharges it with theological meaning for Christians questioning the role of the Mosaic Law after the arrival of Christ.
G0028.portee: Hagar reminds the reader that the Old Covenant, with all its holiness, does not free man but subjects him to commandments that he cannot observe alone. This figure invites the Christian to recognize their own past bondage under the Law, and thus the radical grace that Christ offers by breaking these chains. It also invites compassion for all those who, even today, seek God under the weight of religious performance.

sens: To impose on someone the obligation to provide a service or work without their consent
To compel someone to carry something or to perform a task against their will
G0029.detail:
1. The word primarily means to impose a mandatory service, a requisition: it is the action of an authority that commands and forces obedience. Jesus speaks of it in Matthew 5:41 when he mentions someone who "forces" you to go one mile — it is a requirement imposed, perhaps by a Roman soldier requisitioning a passerby for public service.
2. More broadly, it means to compel someone to perform a specific task, often painful or humiliating. This is what happens to Simon of Cyrene: the soldiers "force" him to carry Jesus' cross (Matthew 27:32 and Mark 15:21). He did not choose it; he is coming from the fields when he is seized and requisitioned for this chore.
G0029.origine: The word comes from Persian and initially evokes the system of royal couriers of the Persian Empire, who requisitioned men and resources on the roads. This system was well known in Palestine under Roman rule, which had adopted it: a soldier or an official could compel a civilian to render a service. The word retains this connotation of obligation imposed by a foreign power.
G0029.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the Synoptic Gospels. In Matthew 5:41, Jesus uses it as an example of an unjust requirement that must be borne with grace by going even further. In Matthew 27:32 and Mark 15:21, he describes the action of the soldiers who requisition Simon to carry the cross: it is an act of brute force, the imposition of a heavy and unappealable burden. In all cases, the word emphasizes the absence of choice and the coercive nature of the imposed service.
G0029.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus himself endured brutal requisition and humiliation: Simon was forced to carry his cross. For the Christian, it also shows that in the face of injustices and abusive demands, Jesus does not preach bitter passivity, but active dignity ("go with him two miles"), transforming constraint into freely consented service.

sens: Container used to hold and transport liquids or solids
Fragile and precious object intended to adorn or preserve
That which receives and preserves something important
G0030.detail:
1. A vessel is a container — a hollow object — used to hold and transport a liquid or substance. In Matthew 25:4, the wise virgins carry oil in vessels to fuel their lamps: the vessel is the practical object that allows them to keep the oil and pour it when needed.
2. A vessel can also refer to a valuable, fragile object intended to decorate a home or to preserve something precious. It is an object that is cared for.
3. Figuratively, the vessel symbolizes that which receives, preserves, and protects something: a person can be called a vessel if they carry or contain something important (a virtue, a treasure, a message).
G0030.origine: The Greek word ἀγγεῖον comes from a root that evokes the idea of containing, enclosing. In Hebrew, it often corresponds to the word כְּלִי (kélî), which also means "container" or "object." These two words share the fundamental image of an object that encloses, receives, and preserves.
G0030.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 25:4, in the parable of the ten virgins. The wise virgins carry oil in vessels to maintain the light of their lamps while waiting for the bridegroom. The context shows that the vessel is a useful and necessary object, which makes the difference between wisdom and folly: it is by bringing vessels of oil that the virgins prepare for the long and uncertain journey.
G0030.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on spiritual preparation. Just as the wise virgins equip themselves with vessels of oil to avoid being caught off guard, the believer must prepare and equip themselves to persevere in their faith. The vessel reminds us that wisdom consists of planning, of providing the necessary resources to stand firm when the time comes.

sens: What is communicated, transmitted from one person to another: news, information content
What is publicly proclaimed, announced to a group to be heard and received
The teaching transmitted in the Christian faith, particularly the content of divine revelation
G0031.detail:
1. A message is a communication transmitted: it is the information, the news that is carried from a sender to a recipient. In 1 John 1:5, it is "the message we have heard from him," that is, what John and the apostles received from Jesus and the Father regarding God.
2. It is also what is proclaimed, solemnly announced to listeners so that they may receive and adhere to it. In 1 John 3:11, it refers to the message "that you have heard from the beginning," the command to love one another that Christians have heard since the beginning of their faith.
3. In the biblical context, it is the Christian teaching itself, the content of the revelation that God makes known through his messengers — the word comes from "angel," meaning messenger.
G0031.origine: The word comes from ἄγγελος (angelos), "messenger" or "angel." Ἀγγελία thus literally means "what a messenger brings," or "the function of a messenger." The verb ἀγγέλλω (angellô) means "to announce, to report." In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates שְׁמוּעָה (shemouah), which means "news, report, rumor," that is, something that is heard and retransmitted.
G0031.emploi: The word angelia appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the first letter of John. In 1 John 1:5, it refers to the fundamental news of the revelation: what John received from Christ and the Father, namely that God is light. In 1 John 3:11, it refers to the essential Christian message heard "from the beginning," the command of brotherly love. In both cases, it is a content of teaching that has been received and must be transmitted to the readers — a word from God that engages the entire life of the believer.
G0031.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Christian faith is based on a message received and transmitted: it is not personal speculation, but news that comes from God through his messengers. Understanding "angelia" means grasping that becoming a Christian is to welcome a specific word, content, revelation — first that God is light, then that we must love one another. This faithful transmission of the message remains at the heart of the life of the Church.

sens: Messenger sent to convey an order or news
Celestial spiritual being in the service of God, executing His will among men
Supernatural creature that worships and glorifies God
Symbolic figure or representative of a church or community of believers
G0032G.detail:
1. In the simplest sense, an angel is a messenger — someone sent to make known news or an order. Thus, the angel Gabriel is sent to Mary to announce great news (Luke 1:26). This is the original meaning of the Greek word, which literally means "one who is sent."
2. But in the Bible, this messenger is not a man: it is a spiritual being, an inhabitant of heaven who belongs to the invisible world of God. Angels carry out divine will on earth and among men — they protect, warn, and execute God's judgments. The angel who appears to Joseph in a dream to reassure him is a perfect example (Matthew 1:20).
3. Angels are also presented as worshipers and glorifiers of God: they serve before His throne, praise His glory, and celebrate His works. In Revelation, John sees myriads of angels around the throne of God, and he hears their voices singing (Revelation 5:11).
4. In Revelation, the word "angel" also symbolically designates the representative or spirit of a local church, as if each community of believers had a celestial figure that embodies it in the eyes of God (Revelation 1:20-2:1; this meaning remains debated).
G0032G.origine: The Greek word ἄγγελος comes from a root meaning "to send, to bring a message." In Hebrew, it corresponds to the word מַלְאָךְ (malakh), which literally means "sent one" or "messenger." The same Hebrew root can designate a human messenger or a messenger of God; the Greeks who translated the Old Testament (the Septuagint) chose the word ἄγγελος to translate this Hebrew term, especially when it referred to a supernatural messenger. The image is that of a mission entrusted to someone who is sent.
G0032G.emploi: The word appears about 172 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. It is first used for messenger angels who appear to men — to Joseph (Matthew 1:20), to Zechariah (Luke 1:11-19), to Cornelius (Acts 10:3-7) — to convey divine instructions. Matthew and Luke also speak of them as guardians and protectors: they serve in the background of the history of salvation. Revelation abundantly uses the term to show angels as worshipers of the throne of God (Revelation 5:11) and as executors of divine plans in the last times. Paul and the Epistle to the Hebrews mention them to remind that believers will live like them beyond this life. A particular meaning, in Revelation, designates the "angel" of a church, probably its leader or spiritual genius.
G0032G.portee: For the Christian reader, angels remind us that God does not reign alone, but is surrounded by beings who obey Him and execute His will. Their presence in the Bible brings peace: they watch over the faithful, warn them of danger, and endlessly celebrate God. Understanding that there is an invisible but real spiritual world helps the believer not to confine themselves to the visible and to see God's hand at work beyond what they can touch. Finally, angels embody an unwavering obedience to God — they are a model of what it means to do His will.

sens: person sent to deliver a message
celestial spiritual being in the service of God
invisible creature that executes God's will
spirit tasked with protecting or accusing
G0032H.detail:
1. In its primary sense, an angel is simply a messenger, someone sent to convey news or accomplish a mission. John the Baptist sends messengers to ask Jesus if he is the one who is to come (Luke 7:24); Jesus himself sends messengers ahead of him to a Samaritan village (Luke 9:52). It is a simple act of transmission.
2. However, in the Bible, "angel" primarily refers to a spiritual being, a celestial creature that belongs to God's invisible realm. These beings do not have bodies like humans; they are spirits dwelling near God.
3. Angels act as servants and soldiers of God. They carry out His orders: announcing a birth (Luke 1:11), protecting someone in danger (Matthew 4:6), or delivering urgent messages to humans about divine will.
4. Sometimes an angel can be a hostile power, a "messenger of Satan" who torments, as Paul refers to as a "thorn in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:7) — a spiritual adversary sent to humiliate him and prevent him from becoming conceited.
G0032H.origine: The Greek word "angelos" comes from a root meaning "to send" or "to bring a message." This is exactly the original image: one who is sent. In ancient Greek, the word initially referred to ordinary messengers (a servant, a herald). But when translating the Old Testament into Greek, "angelos" was used to render the Hebrew word "malakh" (מַלְאָךְ), which also means "sent one" or "messenger of God." This usage specialized it: the word gradually took on the meaning of a celestial being, a spiritual servant of God.
G0032H.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the provided usages, with two distinct meanings. First, the ordinary sense of "human messenger": John the Baptist sends messengers (Luke 7:24), Jesus sends messengers (Luke 9:52; Mark 1:2), John sends envoys (Luke 7:27; Matthew 11:10). These passages show the word in its concrete and historical usage. Secondly, the sense of celestial creature: the angels of Satan who torment (2 Corinthians 12:7), and the angel who speaks to Zechariah (Luke 1:11, implicit). The Segond translates the same Greek word sometimes as "messenger" or "sent one" (when referring to humans), and sometimes as "angel" (when referring to celestial beings). It is the context that clarifies: if it is Jesus or John who "sends" someone, it is a human; if it is God who acts or speaks, it is often a celestial being.
G0032H.portee: Understanding this word helps the Christian see that angels are not primarily mysterious and terrifying creatures, but servants — just like God's ministers on earth. The word "angel" means "sent one": it reminds us that these beings exist solely for the mission God entrusts to them. This invites us to meditate on our own vocation: we too are "sent" by God to bear witness to Him and serve His purpose. The word also speaks to us of the reality of the invisible world, and the fact that God never leaves us alone — He sends His messengers to meet us, even in moments of fear or doubt.

sens: group of animals of the same species living together
group of domesticated animals kept or raised
G0034.detail:
1. A herd is a group of animals of the same kind that graze or live together. In the Gospel accounts, it always refers to a herd of pigs: "There was a large herd of pigs feeding some distance from them" (Matthew 8:30). The word designates the entire group, not each animal taken individually.
2. By extension, the herd can also refer to the animals themselves collectively, as shown in the expression "entered the pigs" (Matthew 8:32), where we see demons entering the bodies of the pigs that make up the herd. The text emphasizes the unity of the group: "the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea" (Matthew 8:32).
G0034.origine: The Greek word agelē comes from the verb agô (to lead, to drive). A herd is therefore literally a group of animals that are led or driven together. In Hebrew, the word 'éder (עֵדֶר) often corresponds to this concept in the Greek Old Testament: it also designates a group of animals that are kept or grazed.
