G0034.emploi: The word appears seven times in the New Testament, exclusively in the first three Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke), all in the miraculous account where Jesus casts out demons from the man of Gadara. Each Gospel mentions this herd of pigs: first the herd grazing peacefully on the mountain (Matthew 8:30; Mark 5:11; Luke 8:32), then the demons pleading to enter (Matthew 8:31; Luke 8:32), and finally the entire herd rushing into the sea (Matthew 8:32; Mark 5:13). The narrative's emphasis on "the herd" highlights the material disaster caused by the miracle: about two thousand pigs perish (Mark 5:13).
G0034.portee: This word reminds us that the physical world—including animals and material possessions—is subject to the authority of Jesus. The herd of pigs destroyed in an instant illustrates Christ's extraordinary power over all creatures and unclean spirits. For the reader, it also shows the cost of deliverance: Jesus frees the possessed man, but the material destruction that results raises questions about the real cost of our healings and freedoms.

sens: whose ancestry is unknown
whose lineage is not recorded
devoid of established pedigree
G0035.detail:
1. This word refers to someone whose ancestors are unknown or whose genealogy has not been recorded in the registers. In Hebrews 7:3, it applies to Melchizedek: the text emphasizes that we have no document detailing his father, mother, or family origins — a striking absence in a culture where genealogy was fundamental to establish authority and legitimacy, especially for a priest.
2. The word also expresses the idea of an absence of genealogical trace, a void in the records: Melchizedek suddenly appears in biblical history (in Genesis 14) without known family antecedents, which underscores the mystery of his person and prepares the comparison with Christ.
G0035.origine: The word is formed from the Greek prefix "a-" (negation) and the verb "genealogeo" (to establish genealogy), itself derived from the noun "genealogy" (list of ancestors). The root expresses the recording or documentation of lineages. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this type of word opposes the central Jewish practice: maintaining and transmitting in writing the lineage of a family or tribe, as is the case for the Levitical priesthood.
G0035.emploi: The word appears only once in Hebrews 7:3, in the discussion on the superiority of Melchizedek as a figure of Christ's priesthood. The apostle emphasizes that Melchizedek is "without father, without mother, without genealogy": this triple negation creates a striking contrast with the Jewish practice that required a traced genealogy to legitimize a priest (cf. Nehemiah 7:64, where priests are excluded from the priesthood due to lack of established genealogy). The absence of genealogy for Melchizedek is not a flaw, but a uniqueness that highlights his singularity and his foreshadowing of Christ's eternal priesthood, which does not need to demonstrate legitimacy through human lineage.
G0035.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the nature of Christ's priesthood: unlike the Levitical priests, who had to prove their right through their genealogy, Jesus establishes His authority as a priest not through His earthly descent, but through His resurrection and permanent character. It is a lesson on how God transcends human criteria of authority and legitimacy.

sens: Of low birth, without noble origin
Despicable, unworthy, of no value in the eyes of the world
G0036.detail:
1. The word describes someone of low extraction, without noble family or high social status. It is the opposite of well-born, of one who enjoys an honorable position. In 1 Corinthians 1:28, Paul speaks of the "vile things of the world," meaning what society rejects as unworthy or unimportant.
2. More broadly, it means despicable or worthless: what is vile does not deserve esteem, honor, or consideration. It is what the world looks down upon, what it belittles or scorns. Paul uses this word to show how God chooses precisely what humans consider vile to confound their pride.
G0036.origine: The word comes from the Greek γένος (genḗ), which means "birth" or "family." The prefix "a-" marks negation: "without worthy birth" or "without noble extraction." In classical Greek, it was a social term that marked the absence of honorable status. The antonym εὐγενής (eugenḗs, "well-born") confirms this image of family and social hierarchy.
G0036.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 1:28. Paul uses it in his argument showing that God overturns the values of the world: He chooses the things that the world considers vile — without nobility, without prestige, without dignity — to nullify the things in which the world trusts (the things that "are," meaning those that have weight, importance according to human wisdom). It is a word loaded with irony: what the world rejects as vile, God elects. This contrast highlights the reversal of values that the Gospel brings about.
G0036.portee: This word invites the believer to accept their nothingness in the eyes of the world and to recognize that God chooses the weak, the despised, the "nothing" to accomplish His work. It is a call to humility and a promise: our apparent "vileness" in the eyes of the world is not an obstacle to God, but the very opportunity to manifest His power and grace. For those who feel small or despised, this word says that God sees them differently.

sens: Set apart for God, dedicate, consecrate
Purify and make conform to the holiness of God
Treat as holy, regard as holy
G0037.detail:
1. To sanctify is first to separate something or someone to make it God's property, removing it from ordinary use. It is to dedicate: thus a vessel can be sanctified to serve in the house of God (2 Timothy 2:21), and Christ was sanctified, meaning consecrated by the Father and sent into the world as one who belongs entirely to God (John 10:36).

2. To sanctify also means to purify someone internally and make them holy in their heart and conduct. Through His sacrifice, Christ has purified "forever those who are sanctified" (Hebrews 10:14), removing their guilt and transforming them. This is what is called sanctification: progressively, the believer becomes truly holy, conformed to God (1 Thessalonians 5:23).

3. To sanctify also means to recognize someone or something as holy, treating it with the respect that is due to holiness. When we pray, "Hallowed be Your name" (Matthew 6:9), we ask that God be recognized and honored as the one who is holy, worthy of absolute reverence.
G0037.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "hagios" which means "holy," "separated," "belonging to God." This verb goes back to the fundamental image of separation and setting apart: holiness is not primarily a moral state, it is primarily a relationship to God. In Hebrew, the word "qodesh" (holy) has the same root and expresses this idea of separation. When moving from the Old Testament to the New Testament, the Greek word "hagiazo" retains this dual dimension: external separation (consecration) and internal transformation (moral and spiritual purification).
G0037.emploi: The verb appears 25 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul and the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, and also in the Gospel of John. It takes on several nuances depending on the context: in the Gospels, it often refers to the honor and respect due to God (Matthew 6:9, Luke 11:2), or the divine act of consecration (John 10:36, John 17:19). In Paul, it often refers to the transformation of the believer by the Holy Spirit and obedience (1 Corinthians 1:2, 1 Thessalonians 5:23). In Hebrews, Christ sanctifies His brothers through His unique sacrifice (Hebrews 2:11, Hebrews 10:14). The word can also apply to a believer's partner (1 Corinthians 7:14) or to objects (2 Timothy 2:21), suggesting that holiness extends through contact and engagement.
G0037.portee: This word is at the heart of the Christian life: it reminds us that becoming a Christian means being separated from sin and set apart for God. It shows that holiness is not a personal performance, but primarily a gift from God — it is He who sanctifies, through His Spirit and through the sacrifice of Christ. The believer is called to cooperate with this sanctification by keeping themselves pure. Finally, to sanctify God's name is to recognize Him as Lord, in prayer and in life.

sens: The action of making holy, of dedicating to God
The separation from sin and evil
The state of one who lives in communion with God
The fruit and vocation of the Christian in daily life
G0038.detail:
1. Sanctification is primarily an active process: it is the action by which God separates us from sin and consecrates us to His service. In 1 Thessalonians 4:3, Paul says: "For this is the will of God, your sanctification," as a vocation, a direction that the believer must follow.
2. It also means turning away from impurity to turn towards righteousness. Romans 6:19 beautifully explains this: "present your members as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness" — it is a voluntary act, concrete choices in daily life.
3. Sanctification is the fruit of obedience to God. Romans 6:22 states that those who are "slaves of God" have "as their fruit holiness and as their end eternal life" — this is what naturally grows in a life surrendered to God.
4. For the Apostle Paul, Jesus Himself is our "sanctification" (1 Corinthians 1:30): it is His life in us that produces this change of consecration and purity.
G0038.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "hagiazo" (to make holy), which is derived from "hagios" (holy, separated, consecrated). In Hebrew, it often translates "mikdash" (sanctuary, holy place), the idea being one of separation from what is ordinary or impure to be reserved for God. The suffix "-mos" indicates that it is the process, the action, more than the final state: we do not just say "you are holy," but "you are on the path of sanctification."
G0038.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament, especially in Paul and in the epistles to the Thessalonians, Corinthians, and Hebrews. Paul uses it to describe God's will concerning believers: sanctification is what God calls us to (1 Thessalonians 4:3,7). It is also the result of our union with Christ, both the means (1 Corinthians 1:30) and the fruit (Romans 6:22) of our justification. The word designates sometimes the ongoing process ("present your members to sanctification"), sometimes the intended outcome ("leading to holiness"). It concerns the entire life of the believer: their moral choices (1 Thessalonians 4:4), their obedience (Romans 6:19), their relationship with God (1 Peter 1:2).
G0038.portee: Sanctification reminds the Christian that their faith is not just a feeling or a doctrine, but a concrete commitment of their entire being — their body, their actions, their choices. It is the response to God's call: since we are separated from sin for Him, we must live accordingly, day by day. This word strengthens the believer by showing them that their moral and spiritual progression is not a solitary personal work, but the fruit of a life surrendered to God and the work of the Holy Spirit in them.

sens: Place dedicated to God, particularly the temple or the tabernacle
The innermost part of the temple, the holy of holies, reserved for the high priest
Sacred space where God dwells and where solemn worship is rendered to Him
In a figurative sense, the divine presence itself or the heaven where Christ intercedes
G0039G.detail:
1. The sanctuary is primarily a building or a material space dedicated to God: it is the earthly temple or tabernacle, the place of worship par excellence. In Hebrews 9:1, the apostle speaks of "the covenant" which "also had regulations for worship, and the earthly sanctuary" to show that the old covenant was accompanied by a specific structure and organization.
2. More specifically, the sanctuary refers to the two chambers of the temple: the "holy place" (where the lampstand and the table of showbread were) and the "most holy place" or holy of holies, hidden behind a veil, where only the high priest entered once a year (Hebrews 9:2 and 9:8).
3. It is a space marked by separation and respect: one cannot enter without reverent fear, for it is the earthly dwelling of God. The word evokes both the order of worship and the prohibition for the profane.
4. Spiritually, the word extends to heaven itself, the true sanctuary where Christ entered once for all with His blood: "Christ did not enter a sanctuary made with human hands... but He entered heaven itself" (Hebrews 9:24). The earthly tabernacle was only a shadow of the heavenly sanctuary.
G0039G.origine: The Greek word ἅγιον comes from the root ἅζω (to respect, to venerate), which primarily expresses the idea of a religious fear inspired by what is dedicated to the gods. In Hebrew, it mainly translates קֹדֶשׁ (qodesh), which means "separation, consecration": what is kadosh is set apart for God alone, removed from ordinary use. The Greek family also includes the adjective ἅγιος (holy, sacred), of which ἅγιον is the neuter substantive form ("the holy thing"). The underlying image is that of a sacred separation, a boundary that should not be crossed lightly.
G0039G.emploi: The word ἅγιον appears nine times in the New Testament, primarily in Hebrews 8 to 10, where the apostle develops the comparison between the earthly tabernacle and the heavenly sanctuary. In Hebrews 9:2, it refers to the two chambers of the temple: the first compartment is called the "holy place," the second the "most holy place." It is the technical term of Levitical worship. But the epistle to the Hebrews transposes this vocabulary from the physical to the spiritual: the true sanctuary where Christ presented Himself is not the tabernacle built by men, but heaven itself (9:24). When the author says that "the Holy Spirit was indicating that the way into the most holy place had not yet been disclosed" (9:8), he means that under the old covenant, no one except the high priest could approach God; the death and resurrection of Christ opened this way to all believers.
G0039G.portee: For the Christian, understanding this word helps grasp the heart of the faith: Jesus Christ, through His unique sacrifice, has created direct access to God. The earthly sanctuary, with its rituals and prohibitions, was only a foreshadowing of what is realized in Christ. This transition from the earthly to the heavenly shows how the Christian faith fulfills and surpasses the Law of the Old Testament. Each believer becomes a place where God dwells, thus participating in the holiness of the sanctuary.

sens: The most sacred place of the sanctuary, where the ark of the covenant rested
The heart of the temple, the dwelling place of God's presence among His people
Symbolically, the intimate communion with God, complete separation from the profane
G0039H.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the inner chamber of the tabernacle (or temple), where the ark of the covenant was kept and where only the high priest could enter once a year (Hebrews 9:3). It is the place of the divine presence manifested on earth, the most highly respected and set apart for God.
2. It is also the heart of Israel's worship: the supreme sanctuary where God visibly dwelled among His people. Everything surrounding it (the veil, the bearers of the ark, the priests) carries its holiness by extension.
3. In a spiritual sense, the expression embodies the idea of an absolute separation from the profane, a radical consecration to God alone, and becomes the biblical image of the most intimate and pure relationship with the Most High.
G0039H.origine: The Greek word ἅγιος comes from a root expressing the idea of "religious veneration" and "ritual purity." In Hebrew, it is קֹדֶשׁ (qodesh) which designates both the holiness of God and what is dedicated to Him. The expression "holy of holies" (Hebrew genitive marking absolute superiority) has been taken as is in Greek: it means "the most holy among the holy ones," the pinnacle of consecration.
G0039H.emploi: The expression "holy of holies" appears in Hebrews 9:3 to describe the inner sanctuary of the tabernacle. This is the only direct use of this term in the provided verses. The expression employs a classic Semitic device (the repetition of the superlative) to express the maximum degree of holiness. It recalls a hierarchical order of the sacred: there is the holy (the outer part of the temple) and the holy of holies (the inner chamber, inviolable). This vocabulary structures the entire theology of Israelite worship.
G0039H.portee: Understanding the "holy of holies" helps the Christian grasp what the heart of Old Testament worship was and to measure the radical change brought by Christ. The veil of the temple, which protected this access, was torn at the cross (Matthew 27:51), opening God's presence to all. This word thus anchors a fundamental truth in the real history of Israel: God desires to be close to His people, and in Christ this closeness is no longer reserved for one man once a year.

sens: Separated for God, consecrated to Him
Characteristic of God Himself: pure, majestic, worthy of reverence
Belonging to God or used by Him (places, objects, people)
Sharing in God's moral purity
Ritually or ceremonially pure
G0040G.detail:
1. What is "holy" is first and foremost set apart, reserved for God and His service. In Luke 2:23, a firstborn child is "consecrated" to the Lord: he becomes holy because he now belongs solely to God. This is the heart of the word: a separation, a consecration.
2. God Himself is the Holy One par excellence: His absolute purity, majesty, and glory make Him "holy" in the highest sense (Luke 1:49). Nothing can be compared to Him; He establishes the model of holiness.
3. The places, objects, and people that serve God become holy through this relationship: the Temple is holy (Matthew 4:5), the angels are holy (Acts 10:22), and the apostles and prophets are as well. To be in the service of God is to be separated from the profane.
4. Holiness also means moral purity, sharing in God's justice and purity (John 17:11, Acts 3:14). A holy heart imitates divine righteousness; it is a matter of conduct, not just status (2 Peter 3:11).
5. In the ritual context, pure, unblemished sacrifices and offerings are "holy": it is ceremonial purity that can approach God (1 Corinthians 7:14).
G0040G.origine: The Greek word "hagios" comes from a root that expresses religious veneration and awe before the divine. In ancient Hebrew, it primarily translates "qodesh," which means first and foremost "separation" and "set apart." This image is fundamental: the holy is what is separated from the common, reserved for God. The word has the same root as "hagnos" (pure), but "hagios" emphasizes the relationship to God more than personal purity alone.
G0040G.emploi: The word appears 156 times in the New Testament. It first applies to God Himself in His absolute purity (Luke 1:49, John 17:11). It then qualifies things and places consecrated to God: the Temple, the City (Matthew 4:5), and especially the Holy Spirit (very frequently in Acts and the epistles). It also designates people set apart for the service of God: Christ in Mark 1:24 and John 6:69, the angels in Acts 10:22, the ancient prophets in Luke 1:70, and the Christians themselves in Acts 9:13 and Romans 1:7. In the epistles, believers are regularly called "saints" (Romans 1:7, 1 Corinthians 1:2), marking that they are called to belong to God. The meaning evolves from a ritual status (separation, consecration) to a moral quality (purity of heart and conduct).
G0040G.portee: For the believer, this word reveals that holiness is not primarily a personal perfection that one conquers alone, but a vocation: to be set apart for God, to belong to Him. It is first a relationship before being a conduct. However, since one belongs to the holy God, one is called to share in His moral purity, which transforms all of life. Understanding that Christians are already called "saints" in the New Testament encourages living in accordance with this identity given by God.

sens: Consecrated to God, separated from the profane
Worthy of reverence and veneration
Characterized by moral and spiritual purity
Member of the Church of Jesus Christ
G0040H.detail:
1. The word first designates what is consecrated to God and separated from all that is ordinary or profane. It is the idea of something set apart for God alone, like the Temple which deserves respect because it belongs to Him (Matthew 24:15 speaks of the "holy place"). This holiness comes from the relationship to God, not from the thing itself.

2. By extension, what is holy is that which deserves veneration and reverence because of this consecration to God. Angels are called holy because they serve God (1 Thessalonians 3:13), and prophets because they speak in God's name (Luke 1:70).

3. The word also designates moral and spiritual purity, the absence of evil. When Jesus is called "holy" (Mark 1:24), it emphasizes not only that He belongs to God, but that He is pure and without sin. It is a holiness of character: "But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints" (Ephesians 5:3).

4. In the letters of the apostles, ordinary Christians are called "saints" — not because they are morally perfect, but because they are separated to God by faith in Christ and belong to His Church. "To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those who are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints" (1 Corinthians 1:2).
G0040H.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ἅζω (to have religious respect) and expresses the idea of a sacred separation, a setting apart for God. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates קֹדֶשׁ (qodesh), which literally means "that which is cut, separated." Holiness is therefore not primarily an innate moral quality, but a consecration, a relationship to God. God alone is holy by nature; everything else becomes holy only through contact with or calling from Him.
G0040H.emploi: The word appears 62 times in the Greek New Testament, almost always in relation to the disciples of Christ or the early Christian communities. Particularly in Paul, "the saints" (in the plural) regularly designates believers: "To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi" (Philippians 1:1). It is never a spiritual elite, but simply Christians, called to be holy because called to belong to God. Revelation uses the term for believers of the end times and for the prayers they address to God (Revelation 8:4). Mark and John apply it to Jesus Himself, emphasizing His incomparable purity.
G0040H.portee: This word transforms the understanding of what it means to be a Christian. To be holy is not primarily a personal moral achievement: it is to be called, separated from the world, set apart for God. This gives dignity to every ordinary believer — a servant named Tabitha, unknowns in Rome — which does not come from themselves but from their belonging to Christ. At the same time, this holiness calls the believer to real purity: if you are set apart for God, live as such.

sens: State or quality of one who is separated from evil and consecrated to God
Sacred and pure character of God Himself
Participation of man in divine purity through sanctification
G0041.detail:
1. Holiness is first and foremost a moral and spiritual quality: that of being pure, without stain, separated from all that is impure or evil. It is the state of one who belongs to God and lives according to His standards. In Hebrews 12:10, the term precisely designates this quality that God possesses and that He communicates to His children: "that we may share in His holiness."
2. Holiness also refers to the transcendence of God, to His infinitely pure and holy character, which radically separates Him from creation and sin. It is divine holiness as the perfection and absoluteness of God's character.
3. For the believer, holiness is the goal of spiritual development: to become holy is to progressively conform to God's holy nature, allowing oneself to be transformed by His grace and discipline.
G0041.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "hagios" (ἅγιος) which means "holy, sacred," that is, separated, consecrated to God. The suffix "-otês" (-ότης) creates an abstract noun: it transforms a quality into a state or essence. It is like moving from "holy" (adjective) to "holiness" (noun). This Greek word translates in the Old Testament words in Hebrew evoking separation and consecration to God.
G0041.emploi: The word appears rarely in the New Testament (the dictionary notes only one well-attested occurrence in Hebrews 12:10). However, the notion of holiness is omnipresent in Scripture. In Hebrews 12:10, the context is that of divine discipline: the Father chastens us so that we may share in His holiness. It is therefore a received holiness, a holiness toward which God guides us through His education. The word designates holiness as an abstract quality, a state to which the believer is called, rather than simply the people or things that are holy.
G0041.portee: This word invites the believer to understand that holiness is not an inaccessible perfection, but a participation in the very nature of God. It is built through divine discipline: the trials and correction we receive from the Father aim to make us holy, like Him. It is a powerful call to the progressive transformation of the heart and life.

sens: the state of one who is separated from sin and consecrated to God
the moral quality of one who lives in purity and obedience
the process of sanctification by which one is purified and becomes holy
the final, perfect, and blameless condition before God
G0042.detail:
1. Holiness is primarily a separation: it marks one who is set apart for God, who turns away from sin. Jesus is declared the Son of God "according to the Spirit of holiness" (Romans 1:4), which means He is completely separated from sin, wholly consecrated to God the Father.
2. It is also an active moral quality: holiness is not just a negative purity (absence of sin), but a positive life of righteousness and obedience. Those who purify themselves "from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit" by "perfecting holiness" (2 Corinthians 7:1) practice a holiness that grows each day.
3. It is also an ongoing process: the word describes the Christian's progression toward purity. This sanctification is accomplished "in the fear of God" (2 Corinthians 7:1), which implies constant vigilance and a heart oriented toward Him.
4. Finally, it denotes the final and perfect state: the hearts of believers will be "blameless in holiness" at the coming of Christ (1 Thessalonians 3:13), meaning they will be entirely purified and consecrated on the day of judgment.
G0042.origine: The word comes from the adjective ἅγιος (holy, consecrated, separated), which itself is derived from a root indicating ritual or moral separation. In Hebrew, the close concept is קֹדֶשׁ (qôdesh), the holiness of God that absolutely separates Him from all impurity. The formation of the Greek word with the suffix -σύνη (indicating a persistent state or quality) emphasizes that holiness is a state, a lasting condition rather than a mere act.
G0042.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in Paul's epistles. In Romans 1:4, it describes the holiness of the Son of God, His character as absolutely pure and separated from sin. In 2 Corinthians 7:1, it denotes the ongoing process of purification that Christians must pursue in response to God's promises. In 1 Thessalonians 3:13, it applies to the final and perfect state of believers on the day of judgment. Paul uses this term to urge the faithful to progress in moral purity, imitating the holiness of Christ and preparing for His coming.
G0042.portee: This word reminds the Christian that holiness is not a perfection acquired once and for all, but a path of purification that engages the whole life. It teaches us that God calls us to turn away from sin and to become instruments of righteousness. It also offers us the hope that our present imperfection will give way to complete blamelessness when Christ returns, provided we pursue our sanctification "in the fear of God."

sens: the human arm, limb of the body
the embrace, the hug
the protection, the welcoming power
G0043.detail:
1. The arm is the limb of the body that extends from the body to the hand, characterized by being bent, folded. It is the instrument with which one grasps, holds, and embraces. In Luke 2:28, it is in the arms of Simeon — his folded arms — that the child Jesus is received.
2. But the word especially evokes the action of embracing: the open arm that welcomes and hugs, that holds close. It is the whole act of welcome and affection expressed by this gesture in the Gospel.
3. More broadly, it is also the strength that protects, the power that supports and carries. Simeon's arms express not only his tenderness but also his responsibility as a wise elder who blesses the child.
G0043.origine: The Greek word ἀγκάλη comes from a root meaning to bend, to curve — the basic image is that of the bent arm, the flexed elbow. This is why the word designates the arm in its characteristic form: a limb capable of bending to embrace and hold. It is a vivid word, depicting the natural gesture of the arm that holds something or someone.
G0043.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 2:28, when the elder Simeon receives the child Jesus in his arms at the Temple in Jerusalem. It is a moment of great delicacy: it is in the arms of the righteous, inspired by the Holy Spirit, that the child Christ is recognized as the light of the nations. The context makes the gesture moving and filled with spiritual significance — these are not ordinary arms, but arms carrying an ancient promise finally fulfilled.
G0043.portee: This passage invites the reader to imagine the very act of welcome and protection. Simeon's arms illustrate how one receives Jesus: with reverence, with love, with the assurance that He is the promised Savior. For the Christian, it is also an image of how God welcomes us in His powerful love — not from a distance, but by taking us into His embrace.

sens: a pointed hook intended to catch fish
a fishing instrument attached to a line
G0044.detail:
1. The hook is a small pointed hook, usually made of metal, used to catch fish. It is the basic equipment of the fisherman: it is baited with a lure and attached to a line. In Matthew 17:27, Jesus tells Peter: "Go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up" — this is how fishing is usually done, waiting for a fish to bite and get caught on the hook.
2. The word more broadly designates the complete fishing instrument: the line with the hook intended to capture the fish. It is by this simple means that the fish containing the coin was brought to Peter.
G0044.origine: The Greek word ἄγκιστρον (agkistron) comes from a root meaning "curve" or "angle" — the basic image is that of the curved hook that holds the fish. It is a concrete word, forged on the shape and function of the object: all its meaning lies in its striking curvature.
G0044.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 17:27, in the episode where Jesus sends Peter fishing to find money for the temple tax. It is the only usage in the Gospels. The context is that of an ordinary, daily fishing, and the word carries no symbolic meaning: it is simply the technical tool that is thrown into the sea to catch a fish.
G0044.portee: This passage shows Jesus who knows the concrete realities of the fishermen's lives and treats them with familiarity. The hook also reminds us that God provides for our material needs, even the most unexpected: it is by this humble and simple means that the coin was found.

sens: A heavy device thrown into the sea to immobilize a ship
The set of anchors of a boat
Figuratively, that which firmly holds the soul in place
G0045.detail:
1. The anchor is this heavy, curved marine equipment that is thrown overboard so that the boat remains stationary. In Acts 27:29, during the storm threatening Paul's ship, the crew throws four anchors from the stern to cling to the seabed and avoid crashing on the reefs.
2. The word also refers to the action of deploying this equipment, or the set of anchors of a ship. In Acts 27:40, when the boat approaches the shore, the sailors "loosened the anchors," meaning they detached them so that the ship could run aground freely.
3. In Hebrews 6:19, the anchor becomes an image of what stabilizes the believer's heart: our hope in God acts "as an anchor of the soul, sure and steadfast." Just as the anchor prevents the boat from drifting, hope keeps us firmly attached to God in the face of life's storms.
G0045.origine: The Greek word ἄγκυρα comes from a root evoking a curve or hook (ἄγκος), which aptly describes the curved shape of the anchor. It is a technical maritime term, likely borrowed from a non-Indo-European language. The same image of the anchor — the idea of a solid hold — is found in other biblical contexts to speak of stability and attachment.
G0045.emploi: The word appears four times only in the New Testament. Three times in the account of the shipwreck in Acts 27 — at the heart of Paul's tumultuous journey to Rome — where the anchor is a realistic and dramatic detail: four are thrown to survive the storm (v. 29), it is used for rescue (v. 30), and it is cast off for the final grounding (v. 40). Only once, in Hebrews 6:19, does the word leave the naval domain to become a spiritual symbol: the believer's hope in God's promise is compared to an anchor that keeps them steady and confident when everything around seems to waver.
G0045.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that hope in Christ is not a comforting illusion, but a solid hold, anchored beyond appearances — in God Himself. Just as the anchor saves the ship from drifting and destruction, our trust in God's word stabilizes us in the face of spiritual storms. It is a vivid image to understand that faith is not a sentimental weakness, but a strength that holds us firmly.

sens: Fabric that has not been carded or finished
That has not yet been used, freshly woven
Speaking of a garment: that has not worn out, that retains all its stiffness
That cannot conform to old without tearing it
G0046.detail: 1. The word refers to fabric in its raw state, just out of the loom, before the processes that soften it. In Matthew 9:16 and Mark 2:21, Jesus speaks of a piece of new cloth that one would want to sew onto an old garment: this fabric has not yet been shrunk by washing or softened by use. 2. It is fabric that has never been used, absolutely new from production. The image evokes something that has just been born, intact and full of vigor. 3. Because it has not yet undergone the wear of time, the new fabric has a stiffness that the old fabric has lost; it cannot therefore adapt safely to a worn garment. 4. The figure goes further: the new and the old are incompatible. Putting together what is too new and what is too old creates a tension that destroys one or the other — or both.
G0046.origine: The word comes from the Greek κνάπτω (to card wool), with the privative prefix ἀ- ("without"). Literally, ἄγναφος means "not carded." Carding was an essential step in fabric work: fibers of wool were untangled to prepare them for weaving, and after weaving, the fabric was carded and beaten to soften it. A fabric ἄγναφος is therefore a fabric that skipped this step — a raw, rigid, new fabric.
G0046.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in two very similar versions of the same saying of Jesus (Matthew 9:16 and Mark 2:21). Jesus uses it to illustrate the absurdity of patching an old garment with a piece of new, unfinished fabric. The meaning of the word remains constant: it characterizes the fabric by its raw and new state, incapable of harmonizing with the old. The application of the parable concerns the incompatibility between the new life of the Kingdom and the old religious practices (traditional fasting, for example).
G0046.portee: This image of the new fabric, too rigid for the old garment, reminds the believer that the renewal brought by Christ cannot slip discreetly into the old structure: it transforms everything. One cannot indefinitely coexist the old demands and the new freedom without something tearing. It is a call to accept radical change rather than seek superficial compromises.

sens: Absence of dirt or physical contamination
State of chastity and moral integrity
Innocence and uprightness of heart
G0047.detail:
1. Purity primarily denotes the absence of dirt or mixture — a physical or ritual cleanliness. In 1 Timothy 5:2, the Apostle Paul urges to treat young women "in all purity," meaning without impure intention or inappropriate gesture: it is the purity of behavior and relationship.
2. It signifies moral and sexual chastity, the integrity of one who keeps away from any forbidden relationship or thought. It is a moral state, not just external.
3. Finally, it expresses the innocence of the heart, the absence of calculation or malice. In 1 Timothy 4:12, Timothy must be "an example to the believers... in purity": it is his inner uprightness that shines and builds up the Church.
G0047.origine: The Greek word hagneia comes from the root hagno- ("pure, sacred"), which also encompasses the idea of separation from evil. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates several Hebrew terms denoting ritual or moral purity, notably tahora (purity) and nézir (consecration, separation). The French word "pureté" retains the essence: to be pure is to be separated from what defiles.
G0047.emploi: The word hagneia appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the letters to Timothy. In 1 Timothy 4:12, Paul asks Timothy to become a model of purity, among other virtues, so that his youth does not hinder his authority as an apostle. In 1 Timothy 5:2, Paul prescribes to Timothy to treat young women "in all purity," showing that this virtue must govern relationships between men and women in the Church, especially when there is a risk of malice. The pastoral context indicates that purity is a visible quality, a mark of the moral integrity of God's servant.
G0047.portee: The purity that Paul asks of Timothy is not an isolation from the world, but a moral integrity that earns respect and builds up other believers. For today's Christian, this word reminds us that our testimony rests on the consistency between our words and actions, and on guarding our thoughts and relationships. It is an active virtue: to remain pure is to protect what is good in us and in our relationships with others.

sens: To become pure according to religious law, by performing purification rites
To cleanse one's heart and life from what morally and spiritually defiles it
G0048.detail:
1. To become pure according to religious law, by performing purification rites — In Jewish religion, certain situations render someone ritually impure (contact with death, illness, etc.), and ceremonies allow one to become pure again. John 11:55 speaks of pilgrims who purify themselves before Passover by performing these prescribed rites. Acts 21:24 and 21:26 show Paul purifying himself at the temple by submitting to these legal practices.

2. To cleanse one's heart and life from what morally and spiritually defiles it — Beyond external rites, the Bible also speaks of inner purification: that of our intentions, thoughts, and actions. In James 4:8, we are called to purify our hearts as we wash our hands, meaning to cast away bad thoughts and selfish desires. In 1 Peter 1:22 and 1 John 3:3, to purify means to live in obedience to God's truth and to turn away from sin.
G0048.origine: The word comes from the adjective ἁγνός (pure, holy), which expresses what is separated from all defilement and consecrated to God. In biblical times, purity encompassed both material and ritual rules (washings, fasts) and moral integrity. The word often translates the Hebrew verb קָדַשׁ (to consecrate, to make holy), which shares this dual dimension: one ceremonial, the other spiritual.
G0048.emploi: This verb appears seven times in the New Testament, always in the sense of purification. The first three uses (John 11:55, Acts 21:24, and 21:26) concern Jewish ceremonial purification before entering the temple. Acts 24:18 maintains this meaning: Paul is found purified at the temple. From James 4:8 onward, the word expands to the moral and spiritual purification of the heart, no longer just the body. In 1 Peter 1:22 and 1 John 3:3, purifying one's soul and heart becomes the expression of obedience to the truth and the desire to live holily.
G0048.portee: This word reminds the believer that purity is not primarily a matter of appearance or external rules, but of the heart. It also shows that Christian grace accomplishes what the old law only hinted at: a deep purification of the whole being, possible through obedience to God. It is a call to the progressive sanctification of the Christian.

sens: action of making pure in a ritual sense
action of conforming to religious purity prescriptions
G0049.detail:
1. The word designates the action of purifying according to the rules of the Law. It refers to a purification of a religious and ceremonial nature: performing the prescribed acts or waiting periods to become "pure" in God's eyes, according to Moses' prescriptions. In Acts 21:26, Paul "purified himself" by observing the required waiting periods of the ritual, which shows that it is a concrete, observable, and dated process ("on what day it would be completed").
2. It is also the state or duration during which one fulfills these prescriptions — the time or act that makes someone ritually acceptable at the temple. Thus, Paul enters the temple "to announce on what day the purification would be completed," emphasizing the precise moment when the ritual obligation would end.
G0049.origine: The word comes from the verb ἁγνίζω (to purify), which itself is derived from ἁγνός (pure, holy). This root evokes the idea of separation from evil and conformity to divine requirements. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew נֵזֶר (vow, separation) and חַטָּאָה (purification of sin), showing that biblical purification concerned both ritual status and distancing from evil.
G0049.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 21:26. Paul, wanting to show the Jewish Christians that he had not abandoned the Law of Moses, submits to the temple purification rituals. He purifies himself and observes the prescribed waiting periods to be able to enter the temple and offer a sacrifice. This use is purely ceremonial: it is a practice derived from the priestly code of the Law, respected at the Jerusalem temple during the apostolic era.
G0049.portee: This word reminds the believer that Jesus has accomplished what these rites foreshadowed: he himself has become our true and definitive purification. The rituals of the Law, however important they may be in terms of respecting God, save no one; only the blood of Christ truly purifies us from sin.

sens: to not know, to lack knowledge
to not understand, to not grasp the meaning
to not know the existence or true nature of something
G0050.detail:
1. To not know, to lack knowledge: the verb denotes the complete absence of knowledge. Paul writes to Timothy that he acted "in ignorance" when he persecuted Christians (1 Timothy 1:13) — he did not know what he was truly doing. It is also the state of the high priest Herod or his contemporaries who did not know Jesus (Acts 13:27).
2. To not understand, to not grasp the meaning: when the verb refers to a word or teaching, it means to not penetrate its meaning. The disciples "did not understand" Jesus' words about his death and resurrection (Mark 9:32), even though they had heard them.
3. To not know the existence or true nature of something: in Athens, Paul notices that the inhabitants revere an altar "to an unknown god" — they do not know his true name or true identity (Acts 17:23). Similarly, the apostles could be "unknown" in distant regions, even though they were at the heart of apostolic action (2 Corinthians 6:9).
G0050.origine: The Greek word comes from the prefix ἀ ("not") and the verb γινώσκω ("to know"). It is the opposite of "to know" — literally "not to know." There is a related root ἁγνίζω ("to purify"), which may share a common origin. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb mostly translates Hebrew words like שָׁגָה ("to err," "to stray"), expressing the idea of a lack of knowledge that can lead to unintentional sin.
G0050.emploi: The verb appears 21 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, 1 Thessalonians). Paul frequently uses it to remind of an important truth or to correct a misunderstanding: "I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery" (Romans 11:25) or "I do not want you to be ignorant on this point" (1 Corinthians 12:1). Mark and Luke use it to describe the disciples' misunderstanding of Jesus' words (Mark 9:32, Luke 9:45). Sometimes the word also carries a nuance of moral responsibility: it is through ignorance that one can sin, but one can also act with full knowledge. The Pauline phrase "I do not want you to be ignorant" has become a characteristic way to mark the importance of what follows.
G0050.portee: This word invites us to recognize the importance of knowing God and his mysteries. Voluntary ignorance has spiritual consequences, as Paul emphasizes to the Romans who are ignorant of the true nature of God's righteousness (Romans 10:3). But unintentional ignorance — that in which we act without truly knowing — receives God's mercy, as Paul the persecutor received. Finally, this word makes us realize how important it is to be taught in faith, far from spiritual ignorance.

sens: A transgression, a wrongful act committed without knowledge or intention
A failure to adhere to divine law that one did not know they were committing
A fault of which one is unaware of the guilt
G0051.detail:
1. The word designates an act contrary to the law of God, but committed unknowingly and unwillingly — through ignorance. It refers to unintentional error, unintentional transgression. In Hebrews 9:7, the sins of ignorance of the people are those that Israel committed without being aware of them, for which the high priest had to offer blood on the Day of Atonement.
2. This term contrasts with deliberate and intentional sins: it designates failures to adhere to the law of which one did not fully grasp the seriousness or that were committed out of ignorance. These faults still required a sacrificial offering, as divine law applies regardless of intentions.
3. In a spiritual sense, this word reminds us that no one is excused by ignorance before God, but also that His grace provides for the atonement of even unintentional faults, provided they are confessed and a sacrifice is offered.
G0051.origine: The word comes from ἀγνοέω (agnoéō), which means "to be ignorant" or "not to know" — constructed from α- (negation) and γνοέω (gnōéō, "to know"). It primarily denotes an error born of ignorance. The Greek Old Testament uses this word to translate the Hebrew mishga (מִשְׁגָּה) in Genesis 43:12, which also expresses unintentional error. The Greek word belongs to the vocabulary of atonement and forgiveness of unknown faults.
G0051.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 9:7, at the heart of the description of the worship of the old covenant. The context is the Day of Atonement: each year, the high priest enters alone into the inner sanctuary to offer blood "for himself and for the sins of ignorance of the people." This text shows that the law of Moses already provided a distinction between unintentional sins and others, and that the sacrificial system included the covering of these unknown faults. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews recalls this ancient rite to show how Christ, through His unique sacrifice, has definitively accomplished what the repeated sacrifices could only foreshadow.
G0051.portee: This word teaches that ignorance does not exempt us from responsibility before God, but also that His mercy extends even to faults committed without intention. For the Christian, it reminds us of the importance of sincere confession and awareness before the divine will — and the insufficiency of carnal worship without the sacrifice of Christ to remove all our sins.

sens: Not knowing, lack of knowledge
Absence of moral or spiritual light
Voluntary blindness or heart's blindness
G0052.detail:
1. Ignorance is simply the lack of knowledge, the state of one who does not know. Peter tells the Jews: "You acted in ignorance" (Acts 3:17), as if the crime they committed would not have occurred if they had known who Jesus truly was.
2. The Bible also speaks of a more serious moral ignorance: the absence of spiritual light that leaves the soul in darkness. Paul says that God "overlooks the times of ignorance" (Acts 17:30), showing that humanity before the Gospel lived in spiritual obscurity from which it needed to repent.
3. Ignorance can be voluntary, a kind of heart's blindness: in Ephesians 4:18, Paul speaks of those whose "understanding is darkened" because of the "ignorance" that is in them "and the hardening of their hearts." Here, ignorance is linked to a deliberate refusal to see the truth.
G0052.origine: The word comes from the Greek agnoia, formed from the prefix a (negative) and gnoïa (knowledge, the act of knowing). It literally means "non-knowledge." This Greek root translates in the Old Testament words that speak of straying or sin committed inadvertently. The word carries the idea of an absence, a deprivation of light.
G0052.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always to describe the spiritual state of humans before or without the Christian message. In Acts 3:17 and Acts 17:30, it refers to the ignorance of the Jewish people or humanity towards Jesus and the Gospel, an ignorance from which repentance can free them. In Ephesians 4:18, Paul uses it to describe the moral state of the pagans, whose hearts have hardened. In 1 Peter 1:14, the apostle reminds the converts that they once lived in ignorance before knowing Christ. In all cases, ignorance is never a complete excuse: it is a state from which one must emerge through conversion.
G0052.portee: This word reminds the reader that sin can arise not only from rebellion but also from ignorance and heart's blindness. It invites repentance, for no one is excused by lack of knowledge once the Gospel has been heard. It also shows that God judges with mercy those who act in ignorance, but expects each person to turn towards the light when it is offered to them.

sens: free from ritual defilement, ready for worship
morally innocent, without guilt
chaste, self-controlled in carnal desires
upright, of sincere heart and without duplicity
G0053.detail:
1. In the religious sense first: one who is pure is free from ritual defilement and is in the state of cleanliness required to approach God and worship (2 Corinthians 7:11: the Corinthians showed they were pure in the matter of the incestuous man, meaning without complicity).
2. On a moral level: to be pure means not having committed evil, being innocent before God and men. This is why Paul exhorts Timothy to keep himself pure (1 Timothy 5:22), meaning free from personal guilt.
3. In the realm of feelings and passions: purity is chastity, self-control in the face of carnal desires. Paul speaks of presenting the Church to Christ as a pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2), meaning faithful and upright; Titus 2:5 describes women as chaste.
4. At the level of the heart and thought: purity is the absence of duplicity, of hidden calculation. James 3:17 says that the wisdom from above is pure, meaning straightforward, without ulterior motives: it comes with sincerity and kindness.
G0053.origine: The Greek word hagnos comes from the root hágos (which relates to hágios, holy). It primarily denotes the state of ritual purity required to approach the sacred. In Hebrew, it often translates תָּהוֹר (tahôr), which means pure in both ritual and moral senses. The word has enriched its meaning in biblical usage: beyond mere adherence to ritual purity rules, it has taken on an ethical and spiritual meaning concerning moral integrity and the sincerity of the heart.
G0053.emploi: The word hagnos appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles of Paul (2 Corinthians, 1 Timothy, Titus), but also in James and John. Its usage is almost always of a moral or spiritual nature, never strictly ritual: Paul applies it to the conscience of the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 7:11), to the faithfulness of the Church towards Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2), to the inner purity of the pastor Timothy (1 Timothy 5:22). James applies it to divine wisdom (James 3:17), and John applies it to one who purifies himself through hope (1 John 3:3). The word is also recommended in Philippians 4:8 among the thoughts worthy of a Christian, and Titus 2:5 applies it to the chastity of women. The main nuance of the word remains integrity and the absence of moral defilement, beyond any ritual consideration.
G0053.portee: For the Christian, this word invites them to seek a purity that is not only external but comes from the heart: a clear conscience before God, chastity of affections, sincerity without calculation. It is not about legalistic purity, but an integrity that reflects the holiness of God and prepares the Christian for His encounter. Purity is linked in Paul to faithfulness towards Christ and self-control; it is a fruit of the Spirit that distinguishes the true wise from the one who pretends.

sens: State of being free from any stain, any impure mixture
Chastity, moral integrity in sexual life
Sincerity of heart, absence of hidden malice
G0054.detail:
1. Purity is primarily a physical or moral state of being free from contamination: it is to be clean, without blemish. In 2 Corinthians 6:6, Paul lists the marks of his apostolic ministry, and he cites "purity" as a visible virtue, an irreproachable and transparent conduct.
2. It particularly refers to sexual chastity, the integrity of body and heart in intimate relationships. This is what Paul wants to preserve in the Corinthians in 2 Corinthians 11:3, when he worries that their "purity toward Christ" may be compromised, just as Eve was deceived.
3. Beyond these two meanings, purity is an inner disposition: a heart without ulterior motives, without duplicity, motivated by sincerity. It goes hand in hand with a transparent life before God and before men.
G0054.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "hagnostètos" (pure), which evokes the absence of mixture and contamination. The root refers to the idea of what is separated, distinct, without blemish — a notion very close to the Hebrew "tahor" (pure). In biblical Greek, purity is often linked to the notion of holiness, although distinct: one can be pure without being holy, but holiness includes purity.
G0054.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, and only in Paul's letters to the Corinthians. In 2 Corinthians 6:6, Paul enumerates the authentic marks of apostolic ministry before God: he places "purity" among the virtues that characterize him, alongside knowledge, patience, kindness, and sincere love. It is a virtue that the servant of God must cultivate to validate his testimony. In 2 Corinthians 11:3, purity takes on a more intimate tone: it is faithfulness toward Christ, comparable to that of a virgin toward her fiancé. Paul fears that the Corinthians may be led away from this purity of heart, just as Eve was by the serpent's seduction. In both verses, purity is a demanding moral quality, linked to personal integrity and loyalty to God.
G0054.portee: This notion of purity reminds us that the Christian life is not only a profession of faith but also a visible, transparent, and honest conduct. It concerns our sexual integrity, our hidden intentions, our sincerity toward God and others. It is a virtue that strengthens the credibility of our testimony and our faithfulness to Christ.

sens: Absence of knowledge, understanding
Lack of knowledge of God and His will
State of one who is deliberately or indifferently ignorant
G0056.detail:
1. The word simply denotes the absence of knowledge or understanding — it is the opposite of knowing. In 1 Corinthians 15:34, Paul reproaches the Corinthians for not knowing God, for not recognizing Him, and he calls this a shame for the Christian community.
2. This lack of knowledge particularly applies to God and what should be known about Him. In 1 Peter 2:15, the apostle speaks of "ignorant and foolish men": these are those who do not know or do not want to know God's will and His benevolent action.
3. Ignorance can also be an attitude: that of one who does not want to learn, who remains closed to the knowledge of God. It is a form of sin or at least a serious spiritual deficiency that Paul deems worthy of shame.
G0056.origine: The word comes from the Greek γινώσκω (to know) preceded by the prefix ἀ- which indicates negation. It literally means "non-knowledge." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, a similar expression is found in Job 35:16 (בִּבְלִי־דַּעַת, "without knowledge"), where the lack of wisdom in relation to God characterizes those who do not seek Him.
G0056.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In 1 Corinthians 15:34, Paul uses it to reproach some Corinthians for living as if they did not know God — it is a call to spiritual awakening and repentance. In 1 Peter 2:15, it is applied to non-Christians, to worldly men who, ignorant of the true God, react with false accusations and foolish acts against Christians. In both cases, ignorance is presented as a serious spiritual state, hindering the relationship with God and producing evil.
G0056.portee: This word reminds the Christian that knowing God is not optional, but essential. It highlights the moral responsibility attached to knowledge: not knowing God, or pretending not to know Him, is sin. For the believer, it is a call to deepen their knowledge of God through Scripture and prayer, and to never pretend to be ignorant of Him.

sens: Not known, ignored
Escaping knowledge, mysterious
G0057.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes what is not known or recognized: something or someone that is ignored, not identified or understood. In Athens, Paul discovers an altar dedicated "to an unknown god" (Acts 17:23): the Athenians paid homage to a deity without knowing who it was or how to call it, for fear of forgetting or offending some god.
2. In a deeper sense, the word evokes what escapes human knowledge, what remains hidden or inaccessible to ordinary understanding. The inscription on the Athenian altar symbolizes precisely this abyss: men worship without knowing what they worship, until the Gospel reveals who this God is that they sought blindly.
G0057.origine: The Greek word comes from the negation ἀ- ("not") and γινώσκω ("to know"). It literally expresses the absence of knowledge. This root γινώσκω is fundamental in the New Testament for speaking of understanding, recognizing, or having a personal relationship with someone. The compound ἄγνωστος appears rarely, always to designate what remains outside the realm of knowledge.
G0057.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:23, during Paul's speech at the Areopagus in Athens. Paul uses this altar "to the unknown god" as a bridge to present the true God, whom the Athenians worshiped without knowing. It is a moment of spiritual pedagogy: Paul shows that human religion, even sincere, remains blind as long as God does not reveal Himself.
G0057.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the gap between human religious desire and the true knowledge of God. The Athenians worshiped sincerely, but in ignorance; Paul reveals that Jesus is the answer to this unconscious quest. This also speaks to the Christian: our relationship with God is only possible through the revelation He makes of Himself, not through our assumptions or traditions.

sens: open space where people gather in a city or village
marketplace where buying and selling occur
place where people meet to discuss and show themselves
G0058.detail:
1. The public square is the open space at the heart of a city where residents naturally gather. It is a crossroads of life: people come to work, to shop, and to meet. In Matthew 20:3, Jesus sees workers waiting for work, doing nothing.

2. It is also the market, the place of commerce. In Mark 7:4, the scribes and Pharisees meticulously observe traditions after returning "from the public square," where they mingled with the crowd and risked ritual defilement according to their understanding.

3. The public square is primarily a social theater: a place to be seen, noticed, and respected. In Matthew 23:7 and Mark 12:38, Jesus denounces the scribes who "love to be greeted in the public squares" — it is there, visible to all, that they seek glory and human honors. It is a place where prestige matters.
G0058.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to gather" or "to assemble." The public square, by nature, is the place where people gather: it exists only through the presence of a crowd. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, two words designated this space: the term for "market" and the one for "place," highlighting both the economic activity and the social reality of this meeting place.
G0058.emploi: The word appears eleven times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and in Acts. Jesus goes there to preach (Acts 17:17), the sick are laid there to meet Him (Mark 6:56), and children play there (Matthew 11:16, Luke 7:32). It is also the backdrop for religious vanity: the scribes and Pharisees parade there to be admired (Matthew 23:7, Mark 12:38, Luke 11:43, Luke 20:46). In Acts 16:19 and 17:7, the public square becomes the place where troubles arise and where the crowd assembles in a threatening manner.
G0058.portee: The public square in Jesus' context reveals a moral tension: it is a place of service (healing the sick) or vanity (seeking honors). It reminds us that social visibility can corrupt our hearts. Jesus, on the other hand, heals discreetly and denounces ostentation: true honor is not to shine in the eyes of all, but to be faithful to God in secret.

sens: to acquire a good in exchange for money
to purchase something in the market or from a seller
to obtain at the cost of a sacrifice or payment
to acquire for oneself by means of a price paid
to free someone from slavery or debt by paying a ransom
G0059.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: to go buy something at the market or from a seller by giving money in exchange. It is the daily act of acquiring a good: one buys bread, clothing, a field, a shroud (Mark 15:46). The disciples ask Jesus for money to "buy food" (John 6:5).

2. The word also describes the usual commercial transaction: people "bought, sold, planted, built" in the cities (Luke 17:28), meaning they conducted their ordinary business. During the storm, Jesus commands His disciples to go "buy food" (Matthew 14:15).

3. When the price paid is a sacrifice of oneself or a ransom, the word takes on a new depth. The man who found a treasure "sells all he has and buys the field" (Matthew 13:44): he abandons everything to obtain what is worthwhile.

4. The most important figurative meaning appears when discussing the redemption of humanity: you have been "bought at a great price" (1 Corinthians 6:20). Here, "buy" means to free someone who is enslaved or in debt by paying the price of their freedom — and that price is the blood of Christ (Revelation 5:9).
G0059.origine: The word comes from the Greek "agora" (ἀγορά), which designates the market, the public square where buying and selling occur. "To buy" literally means "to do business in the market." In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew "kanah" (קנה, to acquire) and "shabar" (שׁבר, commerce). It is an ordinary word, but it carries a theological resonance when it speaks of the redemption of men by God or by Christ: paying a price to liberate.
G0059.emploi: The verb appears 31 times in the New Testament. In the Gospels, it describes ordinary acts: buying food, a shroud, oils (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John). But it takes on a crucial theological meaning in the epistles and Revelation. Paul asserts that the Corinthians "were bought at a great price" (1 Corinthians 6:20, 7:23): Christ "bought" humanity to free it from sin. In Revelation, the Lord "redeems" for God a multitude from every nation (5:9), and only those who "buy gold" from God can enter His kingdom (3:18). The meaning shifts from human commerce to the mystery of redemption.
G0059.portee: This word reminds Christians that they do not belong to themselves: they have been "bought at a great price," that of the blood of Christ. It is an invitation to gratitude and obedience — to glorify God in their body and spirit (1 Corinthians 6:20). It also teaches that faith in Christ is worth more than all the goods of this world: the Kingdom is like the one who sells everything to buy the field (Matthew 13:44). Finally, it expresses God's redemptive love: He paid the exorbitant price to rescue us from the slavery of sin.

sens: people from the market, without occupation
bystanders lingering in public squares
ignorant crowd easily manipulated
designated days for judicial hearings
G0060.detail:
1. The word first literally designates the people found at the market — those who loiter without regular work, idlers. In Acts 17:5, it refers to "wicked men of the mob" whom jealous Jews hire to create disorder: worthless men, available, without dignity.
2. By extension, the word evokes a crowd of bystanders, people who linger in public squares and places, ready to follow anything. It is the mass of citizens of little value, foreign to serious matters.
3. This meaning is enriched with a pejorative nuance: the mob is the ignorant and fickle crowd, one that can be incited against someone in an instant. Acts 17:5 clearly shows this: these men are bought to sow trouble.
4. In Acts 19:38, the word takes on an administrative meaning: "days" of hearing, that is, the regular days when the court sits. The connection with the market comes from there as well: just as the market is held on fixed days, judicial hearings take place on agreed days.
G0060.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἀγορά (agora), which designates the market, the public square where citizens gather to trade, discuss, or assemble. It is an adjective formed from this root: literally "related to the public square." Classical Greek (notably Xenophon) uses it to refer to the habitual market-goers, those who linger without really doing business — loafers and idlers. In later authors, the word shifts towards an administrative meaning: everything related to public life, including the judicial hearings that often took place there.
G0060.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts. In Acts 17:5, it describes despicable men of the crowd, without social status, whom jealous Jews bribe to create a riot against Paul — it carries the pejorative sense of ignorant and venal bystanders. In Acts 19:38, it takes on a purely administrative and neutral meaning: "the days of hearing" when magistrates receive complaints. The context shows that any citizen can assert their rights during these regularly scheduled days. The word illustrates how Greek adapts to radically different contexts according to need.
G0060.portee: These two uses remind us that the disorganized crowd is easily manipulated: the leaders who bribe it can turn it against the innocent. They also invite us not to confuse true justice — that of regular, open, and legal hearings — with street violence fomented by particular interests. For the Christian, it is a warning: the loud majority is not always right, and formal legality does not guarantee truth.

sens: the act of fishing, capturing fish
the result of this action, the quantity of fish caught
G0061.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the act of fishing, the activity of capturing fish: this is why Jesus says to Simon, "cast your nets to fish" (Luke 5:4), meaning to catch fish.
2. It then refers to the concrete result of this action — the catch: after the miracle, the disciples are seized with fear "because of the catch they had made" (Luke 5:9), that is, in light of the extraordinary quantity of fish they had just captured.
G0061.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "agô" which means "to lead, to guide." The basic image is that of the hunter or fisherman who "leads" towards himself, who brings the game or fish to himself. In Greek, "agra" initially meant hunting in general, before being specifically applied to fishing in the context of the New Testament. It is a word from the family of "agogos" (guide) and evokes the idea of "leading to oneself."
G0061.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the Gospel of Luke, in chapter 5, during the calling of the first disciples. In Luke 5:4, Jesus commands Simon to "fish," that is, to go cast the nets into deep water. In Luke 5:9, "the catch" they made is so miraculously abundant that the nets threaten to break. The word thus remains very concrete and rooted in the daily life of the fishermen of the Sea of Galilee.
G0061.portee: This passage reminds us that Jesus knows the real needs of the disciples and intervenes powerfully in their professional lives. The transition from ordinary fishing to miraculous fishing symbolizes the divine calling: men called to leave their trade to become "fishers of men." It is an image of the radical change that Jesus introduces into the lives of those who follow him.

sens: who has not received formal education or schooling
who has not studied the scriptures and rabbinic tradition
simple, ordinary, lacking literary culture
G0062.detail:
1. The word refers to someone who has not received formal education, who cannot read or has not had access to school. This was the state of most common people in antiquity, in contrast to the scribes and the learned.
2. In the Jewish context, it means more specifically: not having studied under a master of the Law, not knowing the Torah and rabbinic traditions in depth. The Jewish leaders are astonished that an ordinary man, without this training, speaks with such confidence before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4:13).
3. The word also evokes the idea of simplicity, lack of refinement, or culture in a broad sense: someone who does not belong to the educated elite.
G0062.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: the negative prefix *a-* ("without") and *grammata*, which means "letters," "writings." Literally: "without letters." This is why it designates someone who has not learned to read and write, or who has not received formal education. In Greek culture, being *grammateus* (scribe) or *grammata* (learned) was a sign of social status; the *agrammatos* is its opposite.
G0062.emploi: The word appears only once in Acts 4:13, to describe Peter and John in the eyes of the Jewish authorities. It is a striking contrast: these apostles, being Galilean fishermen without formal rabbinic training, nevertheless speak with the boldness and authority of masters. The meaning is clear — they lack the formal education and preparation in the scriptures that the Jewish leaders claimed. This shows how their power comes from Jesus and the Holy Spirit, not from their degrees or academic knowledge.
G0062.portee: This word reminds the reader of a crucial truth: the ability to speak of Jesus and act in God's name does not depend on academic knowledge or human culture, but on a living relationship with the Lord and the action of the Holy Spirit. The absence of formal training is never an obstacle to the Christian mission; it is often in this weakness that God manifests his power.

sens: staying outdoors at night with one's flock
living in the open air without a fixed shelter
G0063.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the act of sleeping outside, in the open air, in the fields — what shepherds do while tending their flocks. In Luke 2:8, the shepherds of Bethlehem "were keeping watch over their flocks by night in the fields": this is exactly the situation, watching under the starry sky rather than going home.

2. More broadly, it means living outdoors without a roof, in nature, which was the ordinary condition of ancient shepherds who could not leave their animals.
G0063.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and is composed of two parts: "agros" (field, countryside) and "auleō" (to spend the night outside, to sleep). The image is that of rustic life, far from houses and cities, entirely linked to the care of flocks in the open countryside.
G0063.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 2:8. Its unique use describes an authentic pastoral scene: shepherds watching at night in the fields near Bethlehem at the time of Jesus' birth. It adds a touch of realism that paints the difficult and vigilant life of flock keepers.
G0063.portee: This mention of the shepherds sleeping outside humanizes the context of Jesus' birth: it shows that the Savior is born in a place where, even at night, simple men remain vigilant and awake. It is also a reminder that God's plan unfolds among ordinary people, those who work and suffer, not just among the powerful.

sens: to catch someone or something by hunting or fishing
to capture using a trap or ambush
to catch someone off guard to make them fall into a trap
G0064.detail:
1. The concrete meaning of the word refers to the action of capturing an animal by hunting or fishing — the hunter or fisherman uses techniques, traps, or his hands to seize his prey. It is the world of animal capture: the cunning of the hunter against his prey.
2. From physical capture, the word extends to trapping people: enemies set a net or ambush to seize someone by surprise, to catch them in the act or to arrest them forcefully.
3. Biblically, it primarily describes the action of trying to ensnare someone through words or actions: in Mark 12:13, the Pharisees and Herodians send men to "trap" Jesus using his own words, that is, by cleverly questioning him so that he contradicts himself or blasphemes.
G0064.origine: The word comes from ἄγρα (agra), which means "game" or "catch of the hunt," and the verb agreuō literally means "to hunt, to capture." It is a vocabulary of hunters and fishermen, ancient and very vivid. In the Greek Old Testament, it is found applied to men who want to capture or deceive other men (Job, Proverbs).
G0064.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 12:13. Jesus has just told the parable of the tenants; the Pharisees and Herodians, irritated by his teaching, decide to trap him: they send men to question him on a topic that is both political and religious (the tax to Caesar) so that he compromises himself regardless of his answer. The word agreuō captures the malicious intent: this is not an honest discussion, but a verbal ambush. It is the behavior of the hunter who silently approaches the game.
G0064.portee: This word reminds Christians of a reality: there are words and actions that aim not to seek the truth, but to trap and discredit. Jesus, who knows the hearts, is never caught off guard. For the disciple, it is also a warning: he must remain vigilant against the ambushes of lies and malice, while keeping the wisdom of Christ.

sens: The olive in its natural state, uncultivated, which produces few fruits
Figuratively, a person or a people without a direct relationship to the promise made to Israel
G0065.detail:
1. The wild olive is the olive in its natural state, without human cultivation. Unlike the cultivated or 'noble' olive, it grows freely and produces fruits of mediocre quality. The image is that of a vigorous but barren or unfruitful tree, as in Romans 11:17 where Paul speaks of a wild olive that could have been pruned.
2. Figuratively, it is a metaphor for the outsider to the promises made to Israel. A non-Jewish believer, coming from a different culture and history, is a wild olive that is grafted onto the noble olive — that is, the trunk constituted by the people of Israel and its promises. In Romans 11:24, Paul emphasizes this rupture: you have been 'cut off from the naturally wild olive' — your original nature — and you have received an unprecedented place in the history of salvation.
G0065.origine: The Greek word is formed from two roots: ἀγρός (agrós, the field, that which is wild, uncultivated) and ἐλαία (elaía, the olive). Together, they literally designate the olive of the field, the uncivilized olive. This metaphor is very familiar to an ancient reader: the contrast between the wild olive and the cultivated olive was a well-known agricultural fact in the Mediterranean world.
G0065.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Romans 11, where Paul develops an agricultural allegory about the relationship between Israel and the Church. In Romans 11:17, he describes a wild olive grafted — an extraordinary agricultural practice — onto the trunk of the noble olive. In Romans 11:24, he insists: this grafting goes against nature, since one grafts the wild onto the cultivated, whereas one would usually do the opposite. These two uses develop the idea that believing Gentiles access a grace that was not intended for their nature, but for that of the Jewish people.
G0065.portee: This image challenges the non-Jewish Christian regarding their unique position in the history of salvation. They do not inherit from the trunk by nature — they are not citizens of Israel nor beneficiaries of the promises of the Torah — but by grafting, that is, by grace. This humility of the 'wild one made fruitful' invites the believer to gratitude and to guard against pride.

sens: That grows freely in the fields, without cultivation
That is violent, furious, aggressive
G0066.detail:
1. Wild honey is that which bees produce freely, in nature, without human intervention — it has not been domesticated or refined. John the Baptist fed on wild honey (Matthew 3:4, Mark 1:6), which testifies to his austere life in the desert, away from civilization.

2. Figuratively, wild describes an unleashed, untamed, and dangerous force: the furious waves of the sea, mentioned in the epistle of Jude (Jude 1:13), are those violent and destructive surges that symbolize the agitation and excess of those who stray from the truth.
G0066.origine: The Greek word comes from ἀγρός (agros, 'the field'). It designates what lives or grows in the fields, far from human dwellings and cultivation. The basic image is that of free nature, not subjected to the hand of man. The word carries within it the idea of a power escaping control.
G0066.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. In Matthew and Mark, it qualifies the honey eaten by John the Baptist: the honey from wild bees, from the desert. This notation emphasizes the asceticism of the Forerunner, his break with urban and civilized comfort.
