In the epistle of Jude, it characterizes the furious waves of the sea, in a passage where the author denounces false teachers and lawless spirits: the wild waves symbolize the agitation and rebellion against the order established by God.
G0066.portee: For the Christian, this word invites reflection on two aspects of life: on one hand, it celebrates the simplicity and detachment of John the Baptist, who draws his sustenance from creation and not from urban civilization; on the other hand, it warns against unleashed powers, forces that refuse to be disciplined by the wisdom and love of God.

sens: King of Judea and certain territories of the Near East in the first century
Man before whom the apostle Paul compares and defends his faith
G0067.detail:
1. Agrippa II is a Jewish king who rules over several lands during the time of the Roman Empire. He is the son of Herod Agrippa I, himself the grandson of Herod the Great. At the time Agrippa appears in Acts, he visits Caesarea with his sister Bernice to meet the Roman governor Festus (Acts 25:13).

2. Paul is brought before Agrippa so that he may hear him defend his faith. King Agrippa attends Paul's trial, impressed by what he hears. During this solemn hearing, Agrippa tells Paul that he is permitted to speak (Acts 26:1), and Paul later recounts what the king replied to him: 'Almost you persuade me to be a Christian' (Acts 26:28).
G0067.origine: Agrippas (in Greek) is a Latin name, Agrippa, borne by several important historical Roman figures. In Judea, this name becomes famous through the Herodian dynasty. Agrippa II bears the name of his grandfather Herod Agrippa I. Although a vassal king of the Romans, he retains real power and great influence with the Roman administration.
G0067.emploi: Agrippa II appears twelve times in the New Testament, exclusively in Acts 25 and 26, during Paul's trial in Caesarea. He is a historically attested figure who reigned from 50 to 93 AD. His role in Acts is that of a principal witness to the apostolic testimony: Festus, the governor, invites him specifically to help judge Paul's case. Agrippa listens to Paul's passionate discourse about his Christian experience and his encounter with the risen Jesus, and he is visibly troubled by it (Acts 26:27-28).
G0067.portee: Agrippa's presence in the Acts narrative shows how the Christian testimony penetrates to the heights of political and religious power. Despite his position, the king is not indifferent to the apostolic word: he recognizes the strength of Paul's argument. His very hesitation ('almost you persuade me') reveals that the Gospel touches consciences, regardless of social status or authority. The reader thus sees that no one, not even a king, is beyond the reach of divine grace.

sens: cultivated or to be cultivated land, divided into plots
expanse of land in the countryside, rural area
piece of land, real estate
G0068G.detail:
1. A field is primarily a cultivated area: the grains that grow there, the wildflowers that dot it (Matthew 6:28: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow"). It is a defined space that can be traversed, and where time is needed for harvesting.
2. By extension, the field refers to the entire countryside, the rural regions in contrast to the city: it is where shepherds live, where flocks graze, where the land is cultivated (Mark 6:36: "send them away, that they may go into the country and into the villages").
3. The field can also be a piece of owned land, real estate that can be sold, bought, or rented (Acts 4:37: a disciple sells a field and brings the price to the apostles). It is a measurable possession.
G0068G.origine: The Greek word agros comes from an Indo-European root meaning open and wild space. In Hebrew, the corresponding word is sadeh (שָׂדֶה), which signifies both cultivated field and plain or open space. The term always retains the idea of worked or workable land, in contrast to wild forest or mountain.
G0068G.emploi: The word appears 34 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew (who speaks of the fields in the parables of the sower and the tares, Matthew 13) and in Luke. It designates either a particular cultivated field (Mark 10:29: leaving fields and houses to follow Jesus), or the countryside in general (Mark 6:36), or a piece of real estate (Acts 4:37). In the parables, the field becomes an image of what produces fruit: the Word falls there, the good grain grows there, or the tares mingle with the wheat. It is a familiar universe to the Israelites, rich in spiritual meaning.
G0068G.portee: For the Christian, the field reminds us that the Word of God produces fruit in a life just as grain does in a field (Matthew 13). It also invites trust: if God cares for the grass of the fields, will He not care much more for you? (Luke 12:28). Finally, following Jesus may cost the abandonment of earthly possessions, including fields, but it is to receive much more in return.

sens: Cultivated land or land intended for cultivation
Rural region, countryside
Parcel of land, real estate
G0068H.detail:
1. A field is a piece of land where plants are cultivated or livestock is raised, an agricultural space distinct from houses and cities. The most well-known example in the Gospel is the potter's field bought in Jerusalem to serve as a cemetery for poor strangers (Matthew 27:7): it is a well-defined parcel, a piece of real estate.

2. The word also more broadly designates the country, the rural region in contrast to the city or inhabited places. It is the open, wild, or cultivated space that extends beyond the villages.

3. In a more technical sense, a field can be a simple parcel of land, a limited property, a possession. This usage emphasizes less the idea of cultivation than that of ownership, of defined land.
G0068H.origine: The Greek word agros comes from an Indo-European root meaning "to go, to move" and originally designated an open space where one can move. In classical Greek, it mainly retains the idea of cultivated or cultivable space. It is the ordinary term in the Greek Old Testament to translate the Hebrew word "sadé" (שָׂדֶה), which has the same meaning: a field, an agricultural domain. Related words include the Greek verb meaning "to lead, to guide," as the field is the space one traverses and cultivates.
G0068H.emploi: The word agros appears mainly in the Gospels and Acts. In Matthew 27:7-8, it designates the potter's field, a property bought to bury strangers: it is a concrete parcel, with a history, that receives a lasting name, "field of blood." The term can also mean the rural region (compare with other Greek words like "chôra" and "chôrion," which express closely related but distinct nuances: one designates a broad territory, the other a parcel or village). The biblical usage remains close to the common usage: a field is always a terrestrial, real, productive, or owned place.
G0068H.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of land in Scripture: the land is never abstract, it is concrete, named, with a history. The potter's field embodies the misery redeemed by the sacrifice of Christ — the poor strangers find a burial place there. For the reader, agros invites us to see God as the one who masters and sanctifies earthly matter, even the humblest, and who brings the outcasts into His people.

sens: Stay awake, do not sleep
Stay attentive, vigilant, watch
Take care of someone diligently
Be spiritually vigilant, morally alert
G0069.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word is literally to stay awake, without sleep: it is the state of one who does not sleep. This literal meaning is in the background of the Greek word.
2. To remain attentive and vigilant in the face of danger or an expected event: it is to watch, to be on the lookout. Jesus asks His disciples in Mark 13:33 to watch and pray because they do not know when the day of the Lord will come.
3. To take care of someone with care and responsibility: church leaders "watch" over the souls of believers and will give an account (Hebrews 13:17), like attentive guardians.
4. In the Christian life, to be spiritually vigilant, in a state of moral alertness: it is a vigilance of conscience and faith, not just of the body. In Ephesians 6:18, watching is accompanied by prayer and characterizes the life of the fighting believer.
G0069.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "without sleep" (ἄγρυπνος), formed from a- (privative) and the word ὕπνος (sleep). In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb שׁקד (shaqad), which means to keep, to watch, to be vigilant with attention. The word has shifted from the physical sense (not sleeping) to the figurative sense (being attentive, vigilant): this is a natural semantic journey, as one who physically watches is thereby attentive.
G0069.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, always in the sense of spiritual and moral vigilance, never in the purely physical sense of staying awake. Jesus uses it to exhort His disciples to vigilance before His coming (Mark 13:33, Luke 21:36): it is an eschatological vigilance, directed towards the return of the Lord. Paul uses it in Ephesians 6:18 to describe perseverance in prayer, and in Hebrews 13:17 it characterizes the work of spiritual leaders. The word always expresses a moral and spiritual alertness, a responsibility before God.
G0069.portee: This word teaches the believer that the Christian life is a watch: no spiritual sleep, no relaxation of attention towards God and His purposes. It calls to take seriously the promise of Christ's return and the responsibility of those who guide other souls. It is a call to conscious and prayerful vigilance, not to anxiety: to watch is to pray, to entrust to God one's very vigilance.

sens: State of someone who is not sleeping, who remains awake
Vigilance maintained during the night or in times of danger
Sustained effort to remain alert and aware
G0070.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of staying awake, not sleeping — a physical state of lack of sleep. This is what Paul lists in 2 Corinthians 11:27 when he recounts his sufferings: he experienced "many watches," meaning sleepless nights, during his missionary journeys and imprisonments.

2. Beyond simple insomnia, the word can evoke active vigilance — staying awake not out of fatigue or illness, but to watch, monitor, remain aware of a danger or responsibility. In 2 Corinthians 6:5, Paul mentions "watches" among his tribulations: it is both the physical exhaustion from lack of sleep and the constant effort to remain vigilant in the face of threats.

3. Spiritually, a "watch" can also symbolize a state of moral and spiritual awareness — the opposite of drowsiness or indifference. This meaning is close to that of "being vigilant" or "staying awake" in relation to God's will.
G0070.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "not to sleep" or "to stay awake." It is based on the idea of the absence of sleep (a-sleep). It is a common term in classical Greek, used by authors like Plato and Herodotus to describe insomnia or vigilance.
G0070.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's epistles (2 Corinthians 6:5 and 11:27). In these two passages, Paul lists the trials he endured for the Gospel: beatings, prisons, troubles, labors, and among them, the "watches." These mentions show that Paul experienced repeated sleeplessness, likely due to the constant dangers of his missions, imprisonments, and the urgency of his ministry. The term thus remains concrete and autobiographical: it describes a difficult physical reality of the apostle's life.
G0070.portee: For today's Christian, these verses remind us that the life of faith is not always easy, and that Paul himself experienced exhaustion and lack of rest. This can encourage those going through periods of watchfulness and fatigue to offer them in communion with the sufferings of the apostle. It is also an implicit invitation to examine our own priorities: are we vigilant for what truly matters, or are we spiritually asleep?

sens: To guide someone from one place to another, physically or by accompanying them.
To take someone somewhere, especially before an authority or a judge.
To guide, direct someone on a path or towards a goal.
To incite, urge someone to act in a certain way.
To spend, dedicate a period of time.
To advance, go (intransitive sense).
G0071.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to physically lead someone from one place to another: to take them with you and guide them. Example: Jesus says, "Take away the stone" and "Jesus said: Bring him here" when bringing Lazarus back to life, or when the disciples bring the sick to Jesus for healing (Luke 4:40).
2. To lead someone before an authority or tribunal, often for judgment or questioning: this is a very common usage in Acts and the Gospels. Pilate "brought" Jesus out to present him to the crowd (John 19:13); Paul was brought before the governor (Acts 23:10).
3. To guide or direct someone towards a spiritual or moral goal: "He who loves me, I will lead him," says Jesus to his disciples (John 14:31). It is the image of the shepherd leading his sheep (John 10:16).
4. To incite or urge someone to do something: God "leads us to repentance" through his kindness (Romans 2:4); the Spirit "leads us" on the path of God (Romans 8:14, Galatians 5:18).
5. To spend or dedicate time: "The days of my life" are measured and spent (Luke 24:21).
6. Intransitively (especially in the imperative), to go, to set out: "Let us go!" says Jesus to his disciples (Matthew 26:46).
G0071.origine: The word ἄγω comes from an ancient root that evokes the idea of movement and leading. It often translates in Greek the Hebrew verbs meaning "to lead" (נהג, nahag), "to bring" (בּוא, bo'a in the hiphil, meaning to cause to enter) or "to take" (לקח, lakah). It is a very common verb in the Bible, at the heart of the vocabulary of movement and direction, whether physical or spiritual.
G0071.emploi: This verb is extremely frequent in the New Testament (68 occurrences). It is found everywhere: in the Gospels, it describes the concrete actions of leading Jesus, the sick, or the disciples from one place to another. In Acts, it is one of the favorite verbs to narrate how the apostles are arrested and brought before the Sanhedrin or the governor. Beyond this literal sense, it takes on a spiritual hue when it comes to "leading" the soul towards God or towards good: God leads us by the Spirit, divine kindness urges us to repentance. The verb can be transitive (with an object: to lead someone) or intransitive (to go, to depart). Its meaning varies slightly depending on the context: "to bring" emphasizes arrival at the goal, "to lead" emphasizes the action of guiding, "to conduct" is more neutral.
G0071.portee: This verb expresses the reality that God is the one who "leads" us. Through it, the Christian reader discovers that their life is not left to chance: God guides it by the Spirit, his goodness urges us to change our hearts, and his goal is to "bring" us to him. It also invites trust: just as the shepherd leads his sheep, as Jesus "led" his disciples, we are in the hands of a Leader who knows us and loves us.

sens: Way of behaving, manner of living
Set of behaviors and habits that characterize a person
Lifestyle reflecting someone's convictions
G0072.detail:
1. The word denotes the way someone lives daily, their repeated actions and choices. It is the concrete image of a person seen in action: their moral demeanor. For Paul, this encompasses what is visible about him — his teaching, his resolutions, his faith, his gentleness — everything that makes up his living portrait (2 Timothy 3:10).
2. It is also the structured entirety of a person's life, the path they take day after day, their habits forged by deep convictions. It is not an isolated act, but a lasting behavior that leaves a mark.
3. By extension, conduct reveals what one truly is: it makes visible the faith, love, and virtues that inhabit the heart. This is why Paul speaks of his conduct alongside his teaching — one does not separate what one says from the life one leads.
G0072.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "ἄγω" (agô), which means "to lead, to guide." Literally, "agôgê" first denotes the action of leading someone somewhere. Transferred to the moral domain, it takes on the meaning of "the way one conducts oneself," that is, the direction one gives to one's own life. The family of the word also includes "agogos" (one who leads), hence the idea of guidance and self-formation.
G0072.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:10. Paul lists what Timothy has "followed closely" in him: his teaching, his conduct, his resolutions, his faith, his gentleness, his charity, his perseverance. The context shows that conduct is inseparable from teaching — it is not just what one preaches, but the life one lives. It is an implicit call to imitation: Timothy must not only receive Paul's words but also observe and reproduce his overall way of life. This uniqueness in the New Testament suggests that Paul chooses this specific word to emphasize the totality, continuity, and visibility of the Christian life.
G0072.portee: This word reminds every believer that their faith is lived out, not just declared. Paul's "conduct" is his best argument: what he is speaks louder than what he says, or rather, what he says gains its strength from what he is. For today's Christian, it is an invitation to seek not only teachers who speak well but models who live well — and to become such a model for those we influence.

sens: Assembly or gathering, particularly for games or public competitions
Place or arena where a competition takes place
Struggle or physical trial, combat in the literal sense
Spiritual combat or moral struggle of the Christian life
Sustained effort, perseverance in adversity
Intense anxiety or concern
G0073.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a gathering of people, especially to attend athletic games or public competitions in the Greek world — this is the original context of the term.

2. It can also refer to the arena or physical place where these competitions and struggles take place.

3. In the literal sense, the word describes a fight or physical struggle: an athletic trial or a direct confrontation between two opponents.

4. Paul transposes this image to speak of the Christian life as a true spiritual combat. In 1 Timothy 6:12, he exhorts Timothy to "fight the good fight of faith" — it is the struggle to keep and defend faith amidst obstacles. In 2 Timothy 4:7, Paul himself asserts, "I have fought the good fight," summarizing his life as an apostle as a courageous perseverance until the end.

5. The sustained effort in adversity is another nuance: in 1 Thessalonians 2:2, Paul mentions the "fights" he faced while proclaiming the Gospel — sufferings, opposition, constant challenges that do not discourage the missionary.

6. Finally, in Colossians 2:1, the same word takes on the color of anxiety or intense concern: "the struggle I have for you" signifies deep solicitude, the inner struggle to intercede and watch over your spiritual well-being.
G0073.origine: The word comes from the verb ἄγω (agō), which means "to lead, to conduct." The basic image is that of an assembly that one "leads" or towards which one "goes" together — hence the meaning of a gathering or public competition. The word gradually enriches: from physical competition to moral struggle, then to spiritual perseverance in the face of challenges. This evolution reflects how biblical thought takes familiar images from the Greco-Roman world — the arena, the stadium — to illuminate the invisible reality of faith.
G0073.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, primarily in Paul and Hebrews. It is almost always used in a spiritual sense: the believer's life, and particularly that of the apostle, is described as a sustained fight or struggle. In 1 Timothy 6:12 and 2 Timothy 4:7, the "good fight" characterizes the Christian's commitment to faith — to keep, defend, persevere until the end. In 1 Thessalonians 2:2, the "fights" signal concrete trials: opposition, suffering, resistance from the world. In Colossians 2:1, the term expresses intense intercession and pastoral concern — an inner and invisible struggle. In Hebrews 12:1, the word takes the form of an "open race," a race to be run with perseverance. Everywhere, the emphasis is on perseverance and courage at the heart of the life of faith.
G0073.portee: For the Christian reader, this word ennobles the life of faith: it is not a passive routine, but a true fight that requires courage, perseverance, and constant determination. Paul uses it to inspire Timothy and the young churches with a heroic vision of faith — not the absence of difficulty, but the certainty that this struggle has meaning and leads to eternal good. The image of the fight also reminds us that the challenges and sufferings of the Christian are not accidents or failures: they are the normal elements of a life committed to the Gospel. At the same time, this struggle is never isolated: it is set within a cloud of witnesses (Hebrews 12:1), a communion of other fighters throughout the ages.

sens: extreme anguish of the soul
intense inner struggle
mental or physical effort pushed to the limit
G0074.detail: 1. Agony is an extreme anguish that seizes the mind and heart — a deep distress in the face of an overwhelming trial. This is what Jesus experienced at Gethsemane: in agony, he prayed "more earnestly," his body and soul stretched to the limit (Luke 22:44). 2. It is also an inner struggle, a battle of the soul against fear, uncertainty, or suffering. Agony is not passive: it involves tension, resistance, a mobilization of the whole being. 3. More broadly, it is an intense effort — physical or moral — pushed to its extreme, where the body and mind are exhausted by pressure.
G0074.origine: The word comes from the Greek "agôn," which means "combat" or "struggle" — like a sporting competition or confrontation. Agony transposes this idea of struggle to the realm of the soul and spirit: it is an inner struggle against fear, pain, or doubt. The starting image is therefore very concrete and physical: a battle, a match, from which the idea of extreme tension arises.
G0074.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 22:44, at the moment when Jesus prays at Gethsemane before his arrest. This unique context is heavy with meaning: Jesus, facing the imminent Passion, experiences a spiritual agony such that his sweat becomes like blood. This is not an ordinary agony, but the most intense possible expression of absolute distress, a struggle of the soul in the face of death and separation from the Father. The word reveals that the Passion was not merely a physical affair for Jesus, but spiritual and mental.
G0074.portee: Luke shows us here that Jesus, in his humanity, experienced true fear, true anguish — not a vague anxiety, but maximum agony. It is a message of comfort for the Christian: our Lord empathizes with our deepest anxieties. At the same time, it shows that faith does not eliminate anxiety, but that one can pray "earnestly" even — especially — when experiencing it. Jesus does not flee from his agony: he goes through it in prayer.

sens: To participate in an athletic competition, to contend for a prize
To engage in physical combat, to fight
To struggle, to strive intensely against a difficulty or opposition
To persevere in effort despite fatigue or obstacles
To fight spiritually through prayer and faith
G0075.detail:
1. In a context of sports competition, the word denotes the intense effort of the competitor who fights to win a victory and a reward: it is the image of the athlete who trains and disciplines himself for the crown (1 Corinthians 9:25).
2. The word can also evoke a direct physical confrontation, a fight in the literal sense: Jesus explains that his servants would have fought for him if there had been an earthly battle to be fought (John 18:36).
3. But most of the time, it means to struggle, to strive with perseverance against adversity: the Apostle Paul fights with the strength of Christ who works in him (Colossians 1:29), and Timothy is urged to fight the good fight of faith (1 Timothy 6:12).
4. The word also evokes the notion of perseverance in effort: "we labor and we fight" because our hope is in the living God (1 Timothy 4:10).
5. Prayer itself becomes a spiritual battle: Epaphras "fights" for the Colossians in his prayers, interceding fervently with God for their spiritual growth (Colossians 4:12).
G0075.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek ἀγών (agôn), which first means an assembly, then an athletic competition or a fight in the literal sense. The verb ἀγωνίζομαι is its reflexive verbal form, evoking the idea of entering into competition, of struggling. This root gives rise in French to words like "agonie" (the final struggle) and "agonizing." In the Greek Old Testament, the word translates the Hebrew שׂוּם (sûm), "to place" or "to set in position for battle," revealing the idea of total commitment of the fighter.
G0075.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the pastoral epistles addressed to Timothy. In 1 Corinthians 9:25, Paul uses it in its primary and very concrete sense: athletes discipline themselves for a perishable crown. Then, the word shifts to a figurative sense: it denotes the spiritual and moral effort of the believer. In the epistles to Timothy (1 Timothy 6:12; 2 Timothy 4:7), it becomes central to express the perseverance of the Christian minister in the face of trials. In Colossians, it qualifies the apostolic work (1:29) and intercessory prayer (4:12). In John 18:36, Jesus uses it to dismiss the idea of physical resistance: his kingdom does not belong to this order of reality. The word thus unites the athletic image with the spiritual reality of the Christian life.
G0075.portee: This word invites the reader to see his Christian life not as a passive walk, but as an active and courageous commitment. It says that faith is not a quiet possession, but a daily struggle against temptation, doubt, and adversity. The word also transforms the view of prayer and intercession: to pray is not to ask weakly, it is to fight with God for victory. Finally, the image of the crown reminds us that this effort is not in vain — it has an eternal reward.

sens: The first man created by God, father of humanity
The common ancestor from whom all humanity descends
The figure of one who represents all humanity in its condition of mortality
The one who committed the first sin and transmitted its consequences to all men
The image of Christ coming to save humanity in contrast with the first man
G0076.detail: 1. Adam is the first man created by God at the beginning: he is the direct ancestor of all humanity, as shown in the genealogy of Jesus that traces back to him (Luke 3:38: "son of Enos, son of Seth, son of Adam, son of God"). 2. All human beings descend from Adam, which means that all humanity shares his mortal nature: "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:22). 3. Adam represents humanity in its state of sin and death; the Bible designates him as a "figure of the one who was to come," that is, Christ, but in contrast: where Adam brings sin and death, Christ brings righteousness and life (Romans 5:14). 4. Adam is responsible for the first sin: he violated God's command by eating the forbidden fruit, which opened the door to death and sin for all his descendants (1 Timothy 2:13-14 recalls his role in this transgression). 5. In Pauline theology, Christ is called the "last Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:45): he is the one who repairs what the first Adam destroyed, "becoming a life-giving spirit" where Adam became a living soul.
G0076.origine: The Greek word Ἀδάμ comes directly from the Hebrew אָדָם (adam), which means "man" or "human." This name is itself linked to the earth (אָדָמָה, adamah, "the reddish earth"), for according to the Genesis account, Adam was formed from the dust of the ground. The etymology thus evokes the humble origin of humanity: created from the earth, destined to return to it.
G0076.emploi: Adam is named seven times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul. In the Gospel of Luke, he appears simply as a link in the genealogy of Jesus (3:38). In Paul's epistles, he becomes a major theological figure: in Romans 5:14, he symbolizes the sinner whose transgression brought condemnation to all; in 1 Corinthians 15:22 and 15:45, he is contrasted with the resurrected Christ (the "last Adam") to show the contrast between the death he introduced and the eternal life that Christ offers. In 1 Timothy 2:13-14, the mention of Adam justifies the order of creation and establishes the respective responsibilities of Adam and Eve in original sin. This usage shows that for the authors of the New Testament, Adam is indeed the first historical man, whose act of disobedience has cosmic consequences.
G0076.portee: The name Adam reminds every Christian that all humanity shares a common origin and that all inherit a condition of mortality linked to sin. But the New Testament never addresses Adam without adding hope: Adam represents fallen humanity, while Christ is the one who breaks this chain and offers new life. Meditating on Adam and Christ helps the believer to understand both the gravity of sin and the power of redeeming grace.

sens: Without paying, at no cost
Without compensation or salary
Without condition or obligation
G0077.detail:
1. The word describes what is done without spending money, at no financial cost. Paul speaks of it in 1 Corinthians 9:18: he offers the Gospel "freely," without asking for remuneration from the Corinthians.
2. More broadly, it is the idea of serving without claiming a salary or material reward. Paul voluntarily renounces his right to receive support from those to whom he preaches.
3. The adjective also takes on a moral hue: to act freely means to do so willingly, out of love for service and not for personal gain.
G0077.origine: The word comes from the Greek δαπάνη (dapanê), which means "expense" or "cost." The privative prefix ἀ- (a-) means "without," which literally gives "without expense." It is a rare adjective, formed to precisely express the absence of cost. It reflects the vocabulary of commercial transactions, but applied to the act of preaching the Gospel in a context where preachers could legally receive a salary.
G0077.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 9:18. Paul asserts there that his personal reward is to preach the Gospel freely, without exercising his apostolic right to be supported by believers. This voluntary choice of poverty and selfless service distinguishes Paul and shows his radical dedication. The usage emphasizes the exceptional and admirable nature of his decision: he could have claimed a salary, but he prefers to give without asking anything in return.
G0077.portee: This word reminds Christians that the most authentic gift is one that seeks no material reward. Paul's example invites us to serve God and others not out of compulsion or for gain, but out of love and conviction. It is an invitation to generosity without ulterior motives.

sens: Man of the genealogy of Jesus according to the Gospel of Luke
G0078.detail: Addi is an ancestor of Jesus in the genealogical line that Luke traces from Jesus back to Adam. He appears only once in the Bible, at the moment when the evangelist lists the descendants of David leading to the Messiah. His name is included in this chain of generations: Addi is the father of Melchi and the son of Kosam (Luke 3:28).
G0078.origine: The name Addi is of Semitic origin, but its exact meaning is not attested in biblical sources. It is a proper name that appears only in the Lucan genealogy and does not appear in the Hebrew Old Testament.
G0078.emploi: Addi appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:28, in the genealogy of Jesus. Luke presents this lineage to show that Jesus is from the royal line of David. Unlike Matthew's genealogy (Matthew 1:1-17), Luke's goes back to Adam and includes different generations, reflecting distinct genealogical traditions passed down by the early Church.

sens: Woman born of the same parents as another person
Woman member of the Christian community, sister in faith
G0079.detail:
1. A sister in the biological sense: the daughter of the same parents. Mary and Martha are the sisters of Lazarus (John 11:3), and Jesus had sisters according to the flesh (Mark 6:3). This is the natural kinship.

2. A sister in faith, in the spiritual sense: a woman who belongs to the Christian community. Jesus says that whoever does the will of His Father "is my brother, my sister, and my mother" (Matthew 12:50), not by blood, but by adherence to God. The Apostle Paul calls Phoebe "our sister" even though she is not his relative: she is a Christian like him (Romans 16:1). This spiritual term unites believers in the same family.
G0079.origine: The word comes from the Greek root that designates the familial bond between brother and sister (ἀδελφός, adelphos, the brother). In ancient Hebrew, the corresponding word is אָהוֹת (ahot), which refers to a biological sister. The Greek form ἀδελφή has taken on an expanded meaning in the Christian community: it is no longer just about biological ties, but a new kinship in Christ.
G0079.emploi: The word appears 26 times in the Segond. In the Gospels, it primarily refers to biological sisters: Lazarus has sisters (John 11), Jesus had sisters (Matthew 13:56, Mark 6:3). Quickly, Paul uses it to refer to women in the Christian community: Phoebe (Romans 16:1), a sister from Colossae (Philemon 1:2). In 1 Corinthians 7:15, a "sister" is a believing woman; in 1 Timothy 5:2, Paul asks to treat women "as sisters." The meaning gradually expands from the biological to the spiritual throughout the New Testament.
G0079.portee: This word reveals the new identity of the Christian: in Jesus Christ, earthly family ties are reconfigured. Belonging to the community of believers creates a deeper kinship than blood. Calling a believing woman "sister" acknowledges her as an equal in faith and integrates her into the family of God — it reminds us that all Christians, men and women, form one body in Christ.

sens: Son of the same father or mother
Friend, neighbor, companion
Member of the same people
Member of the community of believers in Christ
G0080.detail:
1. The brother in the strict sense is one who shares the same parents, like Judah and his brothers, the children of Jacob (Matthew 1:2). This is the most immediate family bond.
2. The word extends to one who is treated as a close friend, like the neighbor who should not be judged harshly (Luke 6:42).
3. The brother also becomes a member of the same people, as when Paul calls "brothers" the men of Abraham's race who listen to the Gospel (Acts 13:26).
4. In the New Testament, the newest meaning: brother designates the believer, the companion of faith in Christ. Paul calls Sosthenes his brother in the apostleship (1 Corinthians 1:1), and the faithful greet each other as brothers (2 Timothy 4:21).
G0080.origine: The word comes from a root that means "same womb, same belly." It relates to words that speak of children of the same father or mother. Greek uses this word to translate the Hebrew term *ah* (אָח), which has the same range of meanings: blood brother, neighbor, compatriot. This extension of meaning reflects the importance of kinship and social bonds in biblical thought.
G0080.emploi: The word appears more than 300 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew, Mark, and Luke who recount the life of Jesus, and in the letters of Paul. It first refers to true brothers: Simon Peter and Andrew, James and John, and the other apostles. Then Jesus broadens the meaning when He looks at those who listen to Him and says, "Here are my mother and my brothers" (Matthew 12:48-49) — whoever does the will of the Father is His brother. The word takes on its full significance in Paul's letters: for Paul, all converts are brothers and sisters. Brotherhood in Christ becomes a principle of equality and mutual responsibility (Matthew 18:15 speaks of correcting one's brother with love).
G0080.portee: This word transforms the understanding of Christian identity. Being a "brother" in Christ is not a vague feeling but a real bond that creates obligations — to love, to bear with, to forgive, to correct gently. For the believer, this means that all who follow Jesus become His family, as important as blood ties. It is a call to solidarity and fraternal communion in the Church.

sens: The kinship that unites brothers and sisters
The affection, tenderness that characterizes fraternal relationships
The collective of brothers and sisters, taken together
The community of Christians considered as a family
G0081.detail:
1. Originally, the word designates the natural bond between brothers and sisters — what unites them by blood and by living together under the same roof. In 1 Peter 5:9, Paul addresses Christians by calling them "brothers": he speaks of "your brothers in the world," meaning all other believers scattered everywhere who are undergoing the same sufferings.
2. The word also evokes the warmth and mutual affection that should prevail among brothers — a natural tenderness that comes from sharing the same family.
3. By extension, "fraternity" can refer to the collective of brothers, taken as a group: it is the collective, the fraternal community in its unity.
4. In Peter's letters, this word takes on a new and rich meaning: it signifies the community of Christians, considered as a large family united by faith in Jesus Christ and no longer just by blood. In 1 Peter 2:17, the apostle exhorts his readers: "Love the brothers" — that is, love this Christian fraternity, this new spiritual family.
G0081.origine: The word comes from the Greek "adelphos" which means "brother." The suffix "-otês" creates an abstract noun (like "justice" comes from "just"). Thus, "fraternity" is the state or reality of being a brother. In the Greek Old Testament, this word is found in the books of the Maccabees, which speak of fraternal friendship and alliances between peoples. It is a word that expresses a familial and relational reality, never technical.
G0081.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the first letter of Peter. In both cases, Peter uses it to refer to the Christian community, this new fraternity created by faith in Christ. In 1 Peter 2:17, Peter lists the attitudes that Christians should cultivate — honor all men, love the Christian fraternity, fear God. In 1 Peter 5:9, he speaks of the "brothers" suffering in the world, inviting readers to feel solidarity with a fraternity that extends beyond their borders. The word emphasizes the unity and dignity of the Church as a new family.
G0081.portee: This word reminds Christians of a transforming truth: in Jesus Christ, we are no longer isolated or strangers to one another. We form a fraternity, a spiritual family that transcends the boundaries of blood, culture, and geography. Peter's call to "love the fraternity" is not a nice suggestion, but a command that deeply engages the believer's heart. Recognizing this Christian fraternity also means committing to the suffering and joy of our brothers and sisters in Christ.

sens: Not visible, unnoticed
Confused, uncertain, lacking clarity
G0082.detail: 1. The word primarily designates what is not seen or perceived: in Luke 11:44, Jesus reproaches the Pharisees for being "like unmarked graves," meaning they are not seen, not noticed while walking. The image is that of an invisible danger, a hidden defilement that affects without being seen. 2. The word can also mean what lacks clarity, what is confused or indeterminate: in 1 Corinthians 14:8, Paul says that if the trumpet gives an "uncertain" sound, one will not know how to prepare for battle — it is a sound that is not clearly distinguished, which is not well understood.
G0082.origine: The word comes from the root δῆλος ("manifest, visible, clear") preceded by the prefix ἀ- ("not"). It literally means "not visible." This negative prefix is found in many Greek words to reverse the meaning (as "atheist" comes from θεός, god). In the Greek Old Testament, the word sometimes translates the Hebrew בַּטֻחוֹת, relating to what is hidden or secret.
G0082.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, in two very different contexts. In Luke 11:44, it describes the graves of the Pharisees: invisible, without visible marks, they become a source of impurity for anyone who approaches unknowingly. It is an image of hypocrisy — the evil that hides beneath the surface. In 1 Corinthians 14:8, it qualifies an uncertain sound, which is not distinctly heard and creates confusion. Paul uses it to criticize spiritual gifts that lack clarity, which do not serve the edification of the church.
G0082.portee: This word confronts us with the danger of the invisible and the confused. The first occurrence reminds us that hypocrisy secretly corrodes the soul; the second warns us that in the Christian assembly, the clarity of the message matters: a word that is not heard or understood cannot serve anyone. It is an invitation to seek transparency and clarity in our actions as well as in our speech.

sens: The quality of being uncertain, which cannot be grasped or held
What is unstable, fleeting, which can disappear
That in which one cannot place their trust
G0083.detail:
1. Uncertainty is what escapes certainty, that of which one cannot be sure. It is the quality of being vague, imprecise, which cannot be fixed or controlled. In 1 Timothy 6:17, the Apostle Paul calls the rich to recognize that their riches are "uncertain": they can vanish, disappear overnight.
2. The word also evokes the instability of what is temporary and fragile. Material wealth, as impressive as it may seem, is always hanging by a thread: an illness, a bad harvest, a foolish act, and everything collapses.
3. By extension, uncertainty characterizes what is not worthy of placing one's hope or trust in. Paul contrasts uncertain riches with the God who gives us "all things abundantly": He alone is reliable and stable.
G0083.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and is composed of two elements: the negative particle "a-" ("not") and "delos" ("clear, visible"). Literally, it is what is not clear, not visible, remaining in the blur. The root evokes the idea of what escapes sight and grasp.
G0083.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 6:17. Paul uses it to qualify riches: they are "uncertain" in contrast to God, who is reliable and generous. It is a warning addressed to those who have wealth, to help them maintain clarity and not to be deluded about the solidity of their material possessions.
G0083.portee: This word reminds the Christian of a simple yet profound truth: this world offers riches, but they are fundamentally unstable and disappointing. The true treasure is trust in God, who alone is permanent and worthy of our hope. For the believer trying to follow Jesus, it is an invitation not to cling to money, but to seek first the kingdom of God.

sens: without a specific direction
by chance
without a defined goal
G0084.detail:
1. At random means "without a specific direction": it is to run or advance without knowing where one is going, like someone charging straight ahead without a plan. Paul says he does not run "at random," but with a clear objective (1 Corinthians 9:26).
2. By chance: this describes an action done without method, at the mercy of circumstances, left to the unexpected. It is the opposite of a thought-out strategy.
3. Without a defined goal: the adverb emphasizes the absence of purpose — one acts without knowing why, without a fixed intention, like hitting "the air" instead of the target.
G0084.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "adèlos" (ἄδηλος), which means "obscure, not clear." The prefix "a-" (which means "not, without") is added to "dèlos" ("visible, clear"), hence the basic meaning: "what is not manifest, what escapes sight." The adverb in "-ōs" derives the idea of an action carried out "unclearly, without clarity," in other words, without apparent direction or obvious purpose.
G0084.emploi: This adverb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 9:26, where Paul uses it to describe how he does not run in his life of faith and service. He contrasts running "at random" (without direction) with running "knowing where to go." The image is that of an athlete: one who trains strikes with the aim of knocking out their opponent, not by hitting the air randomly. Paul asserts that his life, like his preaching, obeys a clear intention, not empty gestures.
G0084.portee: This word invites the believer to examine their own life: do I do things at random, by chance, or with a conscious direction — that of serving God and spiritual growth? It calls for clarity of purpose and intentionality in prayer, Bible study, and service, rather than vague and disorganized piety.

sens: To experience deep sadness mixed with fear and anxiety
To be troubled internally by a difficult or threatening situation
To feel intense sorrow in the face of separation or distance
G0085.detail:
1. To experience deep sadness mixed with fear and anxiety: it is to be seized by a strong emotion that disturbs the whole being. Jesus in Gethsemane "began to feel sorrow and anguish" (Matthew 26:37), describing the extreme overwhelm of the heart in the face of the suffering that awaits Him.
2. To be troubled internally by a difficult or threatening situation: the soul is agitated by fear and doubt. Mark uses the same word for Jesus at the same moment: "He began to feel fear and anguish" (Mark 14:33), emphasizing how the imminent threat invades the mind.
3. To feel intense sorrow in the face of separation or distance: it is also the anguish of one who is far from their loved ones and worries for them. Epaphroditus "was deeply distressed" upon learning that the Philippians knew of his illness, showing how absence and concern overwhelmed him (Philippians 2:26).
G0085.origine: The word comes from a root expressing the agitation of the soul and inner turmoil. It appears in Greek translations of the Old Testament to describe the anguish and distress of the psalmist or prophet. The family of this word in Greek shares the idea of a profound disturbance of being, both physical and moral.
G0085.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the New Testament, concentrated in moments of extreme crisis. Two occurrences describe Jesus' anguish in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:37 and Mark 14:33), capturing the intensity of His spiritual and emotional trial in the face of the Passion. The third in Philippians 2:26 shows how absence and illness create anguish in one who loves and worries. In all cases, the word describes not a simple passing worry, but a deep disturbance that seizes the soul.
G0085.portee: This word reminds the believer that anguish and sorrow are human realities that even Jesus experienced. It validates the emotional experience of the Christian in the face of trials, while showing that going through anguish is not incompatible with faith or obedience. Seeing Jesus "in anguish" in Gethsemane invites us to look at the love and commitment of God that crosses the threshold of His own suffering for our salvation.

sens: the underground world where the spirits of the dead dwell
the state or condition of death and separation
the power of death, personified as a hostile force
the abyss, the void opposed to heaven and life
G0086.detail:
1. The realm of the dead is the underground place where spirits go after death, equivalent to the Hebrew Sheol of the Old Testament. Luke describes it concretely when he recounts the rich man and Lazarus: the rich man lifts his eyes in the realm of the dead and sees Abraham far away (Luke 16:23), thus showing a spatial separation between the regions of the afterlife.
2. The term also refers to the state of death itself, the grip of death on the living. When Peter quotes Psalm 16 concerning Jesus, he states that the Messiah will not be abandoned in the realm of the dead and that his flesh will not see corruption (Acts 2:27, 2:31), emphasizing the dreaded permanence of death.
3. The realm of the dead can be personified as a power or an adversary. Jesus declares that the gates of the realm of the dead will not prevail against his Church (Matthew 16:18), speaking of the gates and the force of death as an enemy seeking to destroy.
4. Sometimes the term simply evokes depth, spiritual lowering. Jesus tells Capernaum that it will be brought down to the realm of the dead (Matthew 11:23), in contrast to being lifted up to heaven, signifying total condemnation.
G0086.origine: The Greek word Hades comes from Greek mythology, where it originally referred to the god of the underworld, and then to his realm. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it primarily translates the Hebrew word Sheol, which literally means "hidden place" or "pit." The root suggests the idea of invisibility and depth. The New Testament adopts this word inherited from Greek culture to speak of the world of the dead, but imbues it with new meaning through the Christian perspective of resurrection and judgment.
G0086.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. Jesus uses it to speak of the fate of cities that reject his message (Matthew 11:23 and Luke 10:15, with the same words about Capernaum), always in contrast to being lifted up to heaven. Luke describes the parable of the rich man and Lazarus by clearly placing both dead men in the realm of the dead (Luke 16:23), providing a narrative image of this afterlife. Peter cites the Old Testament to affirm that Christ, risen, was not held by death (Acts 2:27, 2:31). In Revelation, John sees the realm of the dead personified, associated with death itself, and reveals that the keys to this place belong to the risen Christ (Revelation 1:18), announcing that it will lose its power at the final judgment (Revelation 20:13, 20:14). The word shifts between spatial description and spiritual meaning depending on the context.
G0086.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that death is not the void but a state where the soul exists, conscious and capable of feeling. The Gospel proclaims that Christ alone holds the keys of the realm of the dead and has triumphed over it through his resurrection, offering the Christian the certainty that death no longer has a definitive hold on him. This word invites us to take seriously the reality of the afterlife and the victory of Jesus over death, the foundation of Christian hope.

sens: without a mixture of false appearances or ulterior motives
sincere and honest without reservation
not hiding contrary intentions
G0087.detail:
1. The word describes a wisdom that is not mixed, that has no hidden elements that would contradict its outward appearance — like pure oil without water mixed in. In James 3:17, Paul says that the wisdom from above is "free from duplicity": it does not say one thing and think another.
2. It is complete sincerity, without reservations or hidden calculations. A person free from duplicity does not play a role in front of you: what they show outwardly truly corresponds to what they are and want inwardly.
G0087.origine: The Greek word is formed from the prefix "a-" (which means "not") and "diakrinô" ("to separate," "to distinguish"). The literal meaning is therefore "not separated" or "not distinguished": no separation between what is shown and what is hidden, no hypocritical distinction between a public face and a secret heart. The root evokes the image of a pure substance, without any foreign element that would divide it.
G0087.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 3:17. James uses it to describe divine wisdom by enumerating its characteristics: it is pure, peaceable, gentle, willing to yield, full of mercy. The wisdom "free from duplicity" means that it has no false appearances, that its principles and fruits are in perfect harmony — it is a coherent, honest wisdom that contains no calculation or hypocrisy.
G0087.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that true wisdom — the kind that God gives — is never tainted by false appearances or hidden bad intentions. It is a call to sincerity and integrity in our faith life: to seek honest wisdom, without double dealing, where our words and actions truly reflect what we believe.

sens: without interruption, incessant
which persists day and night
permanent over time
G0088.detail:
1. The word designates what does not stop, what lasts without interruption. In Romans 9:2, Paul speaks of a continuous sorrow that constantly inhabits him, not occasional but permanent.
2. The adjective particularly evokes persistence over time and the absence of relaxation. In 2 Timothy 1:3, Paul remembers Timothy continually "night and day": it is a constant presence in his heart and prayers, with no moment when he ceases to think of him.
3. The word expresses the quality of what never ceases, which knows no interruption or pause, which fills all available time.
G0088.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and carries the idea of unbroken continuity: it is constructed from the negation a- ("not") and a verb meaning "to interrupt" or "to cease." The image is therefore that of a chain that does not break, of a flow that does not stop.
G0088.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 9:2, Paul uses it to qualify the deep grief he bears for his fellow Israelites, a sorrow that never leaves him. In 2 Timothy 1:3, he describes how the memory of Timothy remains constant in his prayers, day and night. In both cases, it is an inner reality — feeling or memory — that nothing interrupts.
G0088.portee: This word invites the reader to consider the depth of Paul's heart: his love for the Church and for those he loves is not a fleeting feeling, but a reality that constantly structures his life of prayer and communion. It shows how true Christian faith engenders lasting and incessant attachments, a devotion that knows no respite or forgetfulness.

sens: Continuously, without interruption
With a regularity and constancy that does not waver
Relentlessly in the performance of an action or a prayer
G0089.detail:
1. The word describes an action that continues continuously, without break or pause: Paul asserts that he mentions the Thessalonians "without ceasing" in his prayers (Romans 1:9), meaning that at every opportunity, without forgetting or stopping, he commends them to God.

2. It also expresses an unwavering constancy in a practice or attitude: the Thessalonians receive the word of God "continually" not physically every day, but with a persistent trust and reception that never falters (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

3. Applied to prayer, the adverb invites a permanent spiritual discipline: "Pray without ceasing" (1 Thessalonians 5:17) does not mean remaining on your knees twenty-four hours, but cultivating a heart's availability to God, an uninterrupted conversation with Him throughout every moment of the day.
G0089.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that means "not to stop" or "not to give respite." The adverb is formed from the adjective that carries the idea of what is uninterrupted and relentless. This notion of unbroken continuity was common in classical and biblical Greek to describe an action or feeling that remains stable and unperturbed.
G0089.emploi: The adverb appears three times in the New Testament, exclusively in Paul's epistles to the Thessalonians and in his letter to the Romans. In Romans 1:9, it qualifies the mention of the believers' remembrance in apostolic prayer. In 1 Thessalonians 2:13, it reinforces the constant reception of the divine word. In 1 Thessalonians 5:17, it becomes a call to permanent prayer, which will become one of Paul's great exhortations to a life of continuous prayer. In all cases, the word emphasizes the absence of discontinuity and interruption.
G0089.portee: This word invites the Christian not to conceive of prayer and intercession as fragmented and occasional acts, but as a continuous dimension of the relationship with God. It also reminds that trust in the word of God should be a constant way of life, not subject to emotional fluctuations or passing doubts. It is an exhortation to daily spiritual faithfulness.

sens: Absence of moral corruption or defilement
Integrity that cannot be compromised or tarnished
Unwavering uprightness in conduct and teaching
G0090.detail: 1. The word denotes the total absence of corruption or moral decay — the idea of a purity that has never been degraded. In Titus 2:7, Paul asks the young minister Titus to show this "purity" in his teaching: no compromise, no lies, no hidden intentions. 2. It is also integrity that cannot be reached or corrupted — an uprightness so solid that it remains intact despite pressures. The passage in Titus emphasizes an example of "good works" consistent with this purity of teaching. 3. Concretely, this means a life and words that remain unblemished, trustworthy, honest in all circumstances.
G0090.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that means "not to be corrupted" or "not to rot" — it opposes firmness and integrity to anything that deteriorates or decays. The prefix "a" (not) and "diaphthora" (corruption) form a compound that emphasizes absence and inviolability. This notion of purity and moral solidity is very close to the integrity spoken of in Hebrew proverbs.
G0090.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 2:7. Paul lists the qualities that a faithful minister must show — "pure" words, integrity, dignity, etc. — so that he does not give cause for criticism and is a true model for believers. The context is clearly that of training a young pastor and his credibility with the Church.
G0090.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds that moral purity is not an option for those who teach or lead: it is a seal of credibility and faithfulness. This also applies to every believer in their daily life — maintaining an integrity that does not wear out, that does not waver under temptation. It is a call to a consistent life, without secret compromise.

sens: To commit an injustice, to act wrongly
To cause damage or suffering to someone
To injure, to harm physically
To persist in evil without repentance
G0091.detail:
1. The primary meaning is moral: to commit an injustice or reprehensible act. It is to act against justice and uprightness. In Acts 25:11, Paul asks if he can be harmed by being delivered without a fair trial.

2. It is also to do harm to a particular person, to cause them injury. Paul tells the Corinthians that he has harmed no one, meaning he has neither deceived nor exploited them (2 Corinthians 7:2). It is the opposite of treating someone with integrity.

3. The word can mean to injure or mistreat physically. In Revelation 9:19, the locusts harm men with the poison of their tails; in Revelation 6:6, it is commanded not to harm the oil and the wine during the judgments.

4. In Revelation, it also designates the condition of one who refuses to repent and sinks deeper into evil: "Let the one who is unjust be unjust still" (Revelation 22:11), meaning that he persists in doing evil.
G0091.origine: The word comes from the adjective ἄδικος ("unjust", literally "without right"), composed of the negation a- and the word for "justice, right." The root thus evokes the absence or violation of right. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this verb translates notably the Hebrew עשׁק ("to oppress, to steal") and עוה ("to act unjustly"), words that emphasize the deliberate violation of justice.
G0091.emploi: The verb appears 24 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in Revelation. It designates either a general moral injustice (Acts 25:11: Paul asks if someone can prove that he has committed an injustice), or an action that harms a specific person (Matthew 20:13: the master asks the vineyard worker how he is doing him harm by paying him the agreed wage; 2 Corinthians 7:2: Paul asserts that he has deceived or exploited no one). In Revelation, the word is enriched: it means "to harm physically" (Revelation 9:4: the locusts cannot harm those who have the seal of God), or "to sink into evil" (Revelation 22:11). The context ranges from the legal to the spiritual.
G0091.portee: This word teaches that the harm done to others, whether material, moral, or spiritual, is a serious breach of God's justice. For Paul, it is a matter of personal integrity and respect for others: one who follows Christ must not harm anyone. For the reader of Revelation, this verb reminds that persisting in injustice without repentance is a form of voluntary damnation.

sens: Reprehensible act, violation of the law
Judicial guilt, that for which someone is accused
Accumulation of faults and sins before God
G0092.detail:
1. A crime or a wrongful act, something that violates justice and the law. It is the concrete act of wrongdoing: in Acts 18:14, Gallio speaks of an "injustice" or a "wicked act" as things he could judge as a Roman magistrate.
2. An accusation brought against someone: that for which they are formally charged. In Acts 24:20, Paul asks that his accusers declare "what crime" he was found guilty of before the Sanhedrin at the time of the trial.
3. The totality of accumulated sins, the guilt that rises to heaven and that God sees. In Revelation 18:5, the "iniquities" of Babylon have piled up to heaven, like a debt that cries out for vengeance.
G0092.origine: The word comes from the verb ἀδικέω (adikéô, "to commit injustice, to do harm"), which is composed of ἀ- ("not") and δίκη (dikē, "justice"). The starting image is that of something going against justice or refusing to respect it. In Hebrew, this Greek word often translates עָוֹן (avôn, "iniquity, guilt") and פֶּשַׁע (pésha, "rebellion, transgression"), showing that crime is not just a simple act, but a rupture with the just order established by God.
G0092.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all three usages provided here. In Acts 18:14, it refers to a reprehensible action that a Roman magistrate could judge. In Acts 24:20, it is a formal accusation brought to court: Paul questions his accusers about the evidence of his guilt. In Revelation 18:5, the word changes register: it is no longer a single crime, but the accumulation of the sins of the great city (a symbol of the power hostile to God), which rises to God and provokes His judgment. The judicial context (Acts) and the eschatological context (Revelation) show that this word covers both the concrete fault and the overall guilt perceived by God.
G0092.portee: This word reminds us that every evil act does not disappear: it accumulates, it counts before God, and it cannot be hidden. For the Christian, this invites awareness of the seriousness of sin not just as an isolated transgression, but as something that adds to a growing debt, until forgiveness in Christ erases it. It is also an invitation to judicial sincerity: not to conceal, but, like Paul, to confront one's accusers openly.

sens: absence of justice, injustice
wickedness, moral malice
act or conduct contrary to righteousness
rebellion against God and His truth
G0093.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes injustice in human relationships — when someone is treated with bias or dishonesty. Paul asks: "Is there injustice with God?" (Romans 9:14), which shows that unjust conduct would be unworthy of God.

2. It also describes the moral state of one whose heart is filled with malice: Paul speaks of people "filled with all kinds of unrighteousness, wickedness, greed" (Romans 1:29), where iniquity is not an isolated act but a disposition of the heart.

3. The word can denote a specific act of evil or sin — a crime, a transgression — as when Judas received the "wages of iniquity" (Acts 1:18), that is, the fruit of his act of betrayal.

4. More broadly, iniquity expresses a rupture with the truth and righteousness of God. Those who "take pleasure in unrighteousness" rather than in the truth (2 Thessalonians 2:12) place themselves in rebellion against God Himself; it is a refusal to live according to divine justice.
G0093.origine: The word comes from the Greek "adikos" (unjust, contrary to right), formed from "dike" (justice, right). Iniquity is literally the absence or violation of what is just. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "awon" (transgression, guilt) and "pesha" (rebellion), which designate sin as a violation of God's law. The family of the word also includes "dikaiôsynê" (justice): iniquity is the exact opposite of divine justice.
G0093.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and in the epistles. It always expresses an opposition to justice or truth. In Paul, iniquity is linked to human sin and condemnation (Romans 1:18, 1:29); it directly opposes the "justice of God" and the new life in Christ. In the Gospels, Jesus distinguishes those who "work iniquity" (Luke 13:27) from those who remain in the truth (John 7:18). The apostle John states that "whoever commits sin commits iniquity" (1 John 5:17), showing that all sin is a transgression. The notion also sharpens: Paul can ironically speak of iniquity as a "debt" or a "wage" (Acts 1:18), emphasizing that evil carries its own retribution within it.
G0093.portee: Iniquity is sin viewed as injustice and rebellion against the righteousness of God. Understanding this word helps the believer see that sin is not just a personal fault: it is an opposition to God's very justice. This clarifies why God cannot ignore iniquity (Romans 9:14), and why confession — admitting iniquity — is the path to forgiveness (1 John 1:9). For the Christian, this word reminds us of the spiritual stakes in the fight against sin: it is not just a matter of morality, it is a matter of truth and allegiance to God.

sens: Who acts or judges without respecting right, justice
Who is contrary to justice, to fairness
Who commits evil, who is wicked or ungodly
Who lacks faithfulness or loyalty
G0094.detail:
1. The unjust is one who does not respect justice: he judges wrongly or acts against the law. When God wonders if it would be unjust to unleash His wrath upon humanity, He questions the legitimacy of His sentence (Romans 3:5).
2. The word also denotes that which contravenes fairness, particularly money gained dishonestly: Jesus speaks of "unjust riches" (Luke 16:11), that is, money tainted by fraud or exploitation.
3. By extension, it qualifies one who is wicked or ungodly, one who opposes God: the Pharisee boasts of not being "unjust" like other men (Luke 18:11), thus designating one who transgresses the commandments.
4. It is also one who is unfaithful or disloyal: one who is unjust in small things will also be unjust in great things (Luke 16:10), showing that injustice reveals a lack of faithfulness at heart.
G0094.origine: The word comes from δίκη (dikè), which means justice, right, just order. The initial letter α- in Greek acts as a negation, like a "no": unjust = one who does not have justice. The family includes δίκαιος (the just), δικαιοσύνη (justice itself), and δικάζω (to judge). It is a classical Greek word to express the absence of justice, in stark contrast to the just.
G0094.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Segond and regularly returns in moral and eschatological passages. It is often contrasted with δίκαιος (the just): Matthew 5:45 contrasts the just and the unjust to show that God sends rain on all without distinction. Luke 16 uses it twice to speak of faithfulness in money and dishonesty. Acts 24:15 uses it in an eschatological resurrection context: the just and the unjust will rise together for judgment. Paul cites it in 1 Corinthians 6:1,9 to warn believers against the unjust, that is, the ungodly. The term consistently retains this dual meaning: one who transgresses the law and one who lives far from God.
G0094.portee: This word reminds the Christian that justice is not an isolated moral issue, but a relationship: to be just is to stand on the side of divine order. The unjust is one who closes himself off to that order. For the believer, avoiding injustice — in money, in judgment, in faithfulness — is a sign of attachment to God Himself.

sens: In a manner contrary to justice
Without valid reason, without deserving what one suffers
In an undeserved way
G0095.detail:
1. The word describes an action or suffering that violates justice: it is to act against what is right, without foundation. In 1 Peter 2:19, Peter speaks of suffering "unjustly" — that is, being mistreated without having deserved it, without having committed any fault.
2. It emphasizes the absence of guilt of the one who suffers: one endures something without having provoked it or without having deserved it. It is to undergo an injustice, an inequity.
3. It is also an adverb of manner that qualifies a deceitful, unfair action, contrary to the rules of righteousness.
G0095.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective ἄδικος (adikos, "unjust," "inequitable"), formed from the negation ἀ- (a-) and the root δίκ- (dik-) which denotes justice and right. The adverb ἀδίκως (adikōs) is its adverbial form. This Greek family translates in the Old Testament Hebrew words such as שׁקר (shéqer, "lie") and עול (âwel, "iniquity"), which all denote what is false, twisted, contrary to the just order.
G0095.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 2:19. Peter uses it to encourage persecuted Christians to persevere in patience when they suffer without reason — not for a fault committed, but simply because they follow Jesus and practice righteousness. It is a word of honor addressed to those who bear reproach with a consciousness of their innocence.
G0095.portee: This word reminds the reader that suffering "unjustly" is never a shame, but can become a grace if borne with a right conscience toward God. It comforts those who are victims of injustice: to recognize that one suffers "unjustly" is to affirm that one has done nothing wrong, and that our faithfulness to Christ is worth more than the false peace of compromise.

sens: Who does not withstand the test, who is rejected after being tested
Who has failed the moral or spiritual test
Who is disapproved by God or declared unfit
G0096.detail:
1. The word first describes something that does not stand when tested: a barren land is reprobate because it produces nothing (Hebrews 6:8). It is the result of an examination that concludes with rejection.

2. For a person, being reprobate means having failed a moral or spiritual test and being declared unfit. Paul says he disciplines his body "lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified" (1 Corinthians 9:27): he fears not holding firm after having preached to others. It carries the idea of disqualification.

3. In Paul, this term carries a serious theological weight: God gives sinners over to a "reprobate mind" (Romans 1:28), that is, to a state where their judgment is corrupted. And false teachers are "reprobate concerning the faith" (2 Timothy 3:8), meaning they do not pass the test and cannot serve God.
G0096.origine: The Greek word is derived from the privative prefix ἀ- ("without") and δόκιμος ("approved after testing"), which itself comes from the verb δοκιμάζω ("to test, examine"). The image is that of metal being put to the fire to see if it is good: if it fails the test, it is thrown away. The Greek Old Testament uses words from the same family for metal dross, reinforcing the idea of waste or refuse.
G0096.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul. It denotes either the refusal of a reality (a barren land in Hebrews 6:8) or the state of a person who has spiritually failed. Paul uses it to warn Christians of the danger of personal disqualification (1 Corinthians 9:27) or to caution against false teachers whose judgment is destroyed (Romans 1:28; 2 Timothy 3:8). In 2 Corinthians 13:5-7, he invites the church to examine itself rather than judge its apostolic leaders, thus reversing the verdict of reprobation.
G0096.portee: This word reminds the believer that faith is not a passive possession but a permanent test: one remains approved only by staying vigilant and seeking God's approval, not that of men. It also warns of the real danger of spiritual drift and corruption of judgment when one strays from divine truth. It is a call to personal examination and perseverance.

sens: Free from mixture or deceit
Without guilt or malice
Authentic, without falsification
G0097.detail:
1. The word first describes what is free from any mixture or impurity: a pure liquid, a pure food, something authentic and unadulterated. In 1 Peter 2:2, Paul compares spiritual milk to pure milk — not mixed with other substances — to show that Christian teaching must be received in its raw truth, without dilution or falsification.
2. The word is also used to describe a person free from guilt, deceit, or malice: someone sincere, who has nothing to hide, who does not act with duplicity. It is the innocence of the heart.
3. Applied to faith or Christian life, the word evokes moral purity: a life without compromise, directed toward God without ulterior motives.
G0097.origine: The Greek word combines the privative prefix ἀ- ("without") and a root that evokes deceit or falsehood. Its opposite would be one who deceives, mixes, or adulterates for profit. The family also includes ἀκέραιος ("pure, without mixture") and ἄκακος ("without malice"). In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates Hebrew terms expressing purity, innocence, or authenticity.
G0097.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 2:2, in an exhortation where Peter invites Christians to desire the milk of the Word as newborns desire it — a milk that is "pure," that is, unadulterated, authentic, capable of truly nourishing. Peter plays on the image of milk to suggest that spiritual food must be received in its simplicity and authenticity, without mixing in false doctrine or hypocrisy. The context emphasizes the sincerity of spiritual desire.
G0097.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Christian faith is not a complicated or adulterated system, but a simple and sincere communion with God through His Word. It invites rejection of any compromise or mixture of lies to grow spiritually in the purity of what has been received from Christ.

sens: inhabitant or ship from Adramyttium, a seaport in Mysia in Asia Minor
G0098.detail: 1. Adramyttium is a port city located on the coast of the ancient region of Mysia in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). When the adjective qualifies a ship, it simply designates a boat that comes from this port or is based there. In Acts 27:2, Paul and his companions board a ship of Adramyttium to go to Asia, indicating that it was an important maritime base of ancient commerce.
G0098.origine: The word is a Greek adjective formed from the name of the city of Adramyttium (Ἁδράμυττος). The suffix -ηνός (-ēnos) specifically indicates that a thing or person comes from a specific place. This type of origin adjective was common in Greek to identify ships according to their port of attachment.
G0098.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:2, during Paul's journey to Rome. Paul is a prisoner, and the Roman centurion places Paul and other prisoners aboard a ship of Adramyttium. This ship must follow the coast of Asia Minor. Its use here is purely geographical and practical: it simply identifies the type and origin of the ship that carried Paul.
G0098.portee: This detail shows the proximity of Jerusalem to the ancient Mediterranean and the importance of maritime routes for the spread of the Gospel. Paul's journey, even as a prisoner, becomes an opportunity for testimony along the way. This word also reminds us that the early Church moved in a connected world, where merchant ships linked the ports of the entire empire.

sens: the sea between Greece and Italy
G0099.detail: The Adriatic is the vast body of water that separates Greece and Italy. It is the sea traversed by ships engaged in trade between the Mediterranean East and the Roman West. In Acts 27:27, it is on the Adriatic that the storm tosses the ship carrying Paul as a prisoner to Rome: the sailors, on the fourteenth night of the storm, begin to suspect that they are approaching land.
G0099.origine: The Greek word Adrias refers to this sea by its ancient name. The Greeks and Romans called it this in reference to the region of Adria, a port in the northern Adriatic. It is a common geographical name in ancient texts of navigation and maritime trade.
G0099.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:27, in the account of Paul's shipwreck. Luke uses it to set the dramatic context of the journey: Paul and his companions are at sea, far from any visible land, when the storm threatens them. This name of the sea provides the reader with real geographical markers and emphasizes the danger that the apostle faces.
